items.title: Weil Gotshal Wind-Down Leaves 830K SF Hole In America's Office Market
items.description: When Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced Wednesday afternoon that it would be shutting down, it wasn’t just the attorneys wondering what would happen to their desks. Law firms have been one of the most active tenant groups this year, signing 12.2M SF of leases during the first half of 2026. But the wind-down of Weil Gotshal — which leases more than 830K SF of office space around the country, according to a Bisnow analysis of CompStak data and public records — could present a challenge for trophy towers relying on lucrative law firm leases to support their rent rolls. “We really have never seen it before,” said Brandon Charnas , co-founder of New York-based brokerage Current Real Estate Advisors . “This reprices law firms as tenants citywide.” Bisnow/created with ChatGPT The closest precedent is Dewey & LeBoeuf, which filed for bankruptcy in 2012 under a heavy debt load. Weil, by contrast, was considered one of the safest tenants in office until this month. Weil Gotshal is one of the country’s most prominent law firms, with about 1,200 lawyers worldwide. It had entered merger talks earlier this month with fellow white-shoe firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher as it tried to play catch-up after losing one of its top attorneys in the ongoing war for legal talent . After those talks fell apart last week, Weil brought in Davis Polk to advise on a potential restructuring. On Wednesday, the firm’s leaders announced it would wind down , a stunning reversal for a firm that was negotiating a merger just weeks ago. Weil didn’t respond to a request for comment. The news caught at least one owner off guard, a landlord who leases to the law firm told Bisnow on the condition of anonymity Wednesday afternoon when restructuring rumors were still swirling. The landlord hadn’t heard from Weil Gotshal, they said, and didn’t know what the firm’s plans were for its space in that office building. The law firm is light on debt but heavy on its lease obligations, according to The Promote . Bisnow ’s analysis of CompStak data and public records found Weil holds 12 leases across 10 U.S. markets. Most are larger than 35K SF, and most were signed or expanded since the start of 2025. The firm leases: 37K SF at 1001 Boylston St., Boston 69K SF at The Crescent , 100-300 Crescent Court, Dallas 3,710 SF at 600 Congress Ave., Austin 390K SF at 767 Fifth Ave., New York City 45,280 SF at 600 Madison Ave., New York City 28K SF at 700 Louisiana St., Houston 100,950 SF at 2001 M St. NW, Washington, D.C. 18,580 SF at 1395 Brickell Ave., Miami 7,950 SF at 600 Montgomery St., San Francisco 59K SF at Shore Center in Redwood Shores, Silicon Valley 26,970 SF at BXP ’s 4 Embarcadero Center, San Francisco 47,300 SF at 1950 Avenue of the Stars, Los Angeles BXP President Douglas Linde suggested during BXP’s Wednesday morning earnings call , when it was still unclear whether Weil would restructure or fold, that the General Motors Building space could be re-leased at much higher rents. “There is a vast gap between where the in-place rent is at the General Motors Building and where we believe or perceive the market is,” he said. But Weil Gotshal is BXP’s ninth-largest tenant, according to the landlord’s most recent quarterly filing . Even for a landlord of BXP’s size, a departure like Weil Gotshal’s could cause problems when the skyscraper’s $2.3B mortgage comes due in June, Crain’s New York Business reported . “Any disruption to the building’s net operating income could impact the refinancing,” Piper Sandler Managing Director Alexander Goldfarb told Crain’s. “If something unforeseen happened, they would have to market the space, find a tenant, and build it out.” Other owners could face similar difficulties. Weil Gotshal is also Hudson Pacific Properties ’ ninth-largest tenant, according to a Q1 2026 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Its other large leases include 69K SF at Crescent Real Estate ’s The Crescent in Dallas and 101K SF at Stream Realty’s 2001 M St. NW in Washington, D.C. BXP didn’t respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Crescent Real Estate declined to comment. It isn’t yet clear how Weil will handle its lease obligations as it winds down or how much its landlords will ultimately recover. Outside of trophy towers, some landlords may struggle to backfill the space after Weil departs, brokers told Bisnow . “You get back a 30-year-old space that needs to be demolished, and you have minimal security deposit from what appeared to be a great tenant — you're in a pickle,” said Darell Handler, president of boutique office brokerage Handler Real Estate Organization. Finding a new tenant for the space might prove tricky unless landlords can lease to another law firm, brokers said. Tech firms, another group of tenants with a voracious appetite for space, are less likely to take former law firm space because they generally want open floor plans rather than rows of private offices, Charnas said. The firm’s closure could also have wider implications for how the office sector views a previously reliable tenant type. Big law firms have long been considered Grade A credit tenants, but Weil Gotshal’s wind-down may change how law firms are viewed by office landlords and how they structure leases, Charnas said. “That is going to be very interesting to see, how this affects security deposits and other means of protection that landlords are going to have to implement going forward, knowing that they can no longer rely on a corporate guarantee of a law firm,” he said. The landlord who spoke to Bisnow on the condition of anonymity echoed Charnas. “It could change landlords’ expectations or strategies around how they securitize those leases in ways that they haven’t in the past,” the landlord said. “I think that it’s going to have a psychological effect on the market going forward,” Charnas said. items.title: Blackstone Mortgage Trust Reports Unexpected Q3 Net Loss
items.description: Blackstone Mortgage Trust reported a $327M net loss for the third quarter, news that sent stocks tumbling. Unsplash/Clarisse Croset Shares were at $9.95 during premarket trading on Thursday. Though they had rebounded during trading hours to just under $11 per share, they were still down 11% over the last month and down roughly 42% over the last six months. As of about 3 p.m. ET Thursday, BXMT shares were trading up 3.75%, or $10.94 per share. Leadership pointed to higher interest rates and challenges facing the office market. "While higher rates and an elongated office recovery impacted our reserves and book value, our watchlist is now at the lowest level since 2019, and the remainder of our legacy portfolio is performing well and shrinking rapidly," Blackstone Mortgage Trust CEO Tim Johnson said in a statement. The company impaired roughly $800M of loans on its books, the vast majority being office assets, indicating that it still has work to do balancing its portfolio, Johnson said on an earnings call Thursday. Leadership said it is still on track to meet or exceed its previously announced goal of reducing office and legacy loans by 40% by year-end. Johnson said higher interest rates will have the greatest impact on some of the REIT's pre-2023 investments, which is why it's prioritizing the sale of older loans. Blackstone Mortgage Trust's total net revenue rose to $141.9M from $132.6M in the same period in 2025 , but interest and related income fell to $280.6M from approximately $346M a year ago, below the Visible Alpha consensus of $293.5M, according to Seeking Alpha . items.title: 'Distress Is Finally Trading': Investors Chasing Big Discounts On Boston Office
items.description: For years following the pandemic, the uncertainty around the office sector left some of the most prominent towers in Boston stuck in limbo and unable to sell to investors that could give them new life. But now, owners and lenders are ready to move on from buildings, even at substantial discounts, and they are being scooped up by buyers who say the price is finally right. Google Maps Synergy's 265 Franklin St. in downtown Boston "Owners and lenders are starting to really understand that their assets may be great assets but have a broken capital stack," Beacon Capital Partners Managing Director Meredith Majoch said this month at Bisnow ’s Boston State of the Market event. "We're starting to see some real liquidity at that end of the market." Majoch said the bidding pool for these types of assets has gotten more competitive. Her firm has sought these opportunities and has lost out on several bids for office properties, but ultimately, she thinks the sales are good for the market. "Distress is finally trading, which is wonderful to see," she said. Majoch was one of several office market players at Bisnow ’s event who discussed the appeal of buying these buildings at such a low cost basis. While many institutional players remain on the sidelines — firms like life insurance companies and pension funds that want steady, predictable returns — opportunistic private investors and foreign buyers see these prices as a prime opportunity to buy low in a city they believe will succeed over the long term. "If we were playing a drinking game where you hear ‘basis’ and drink, we'd all be drunk by now. But it's truly what's going on right now in Boston," North Colony Asset Management partner Drew Pepoli said. "Our investors are pounding down the door, saying, 'Let's buy more. Let's buy more.'" In the third quarter, $2.2B worth of Boston office buildings sold, a 23.7% year-over-year increase, according to Avison Young . Some of these buildings have been trading at well below their past sale prices. Bisnow/Jon Banister Boston Realty Advisors' Jason Weissman and North Colony Asset Management's Drew Pepoli In June, Kendall Capital acquired an 11-story office building at 18 Tremont St. for $30M . The seller, Jamestown , had bought the building in 2019 for $103M. In July, Synergy and New York-based alternative investment manager Axonic Capital acquired the 360K SF building at 265 Franklin St. for $116M from Clarendon Group — 32% less than the $170M Clarendon paid roughly 20 years ago. This week, Rockpoint bought back its 1.1M SF office building at 100 Summer St. at a foreclosure auction, paying $260M , well below the $806M it initially bought the building for in 2019. Young Park , the CEO of Berkeley Garbe, a joint venture formed this year by German real estate firm Garbe and Berkeley Investments, said he is seeing these discounts becoming more common. As lenders are no longer willing to extend loans in hopes an underperforming asset can be turned around, more properties are coming to the market. "I'm encouraged because I see some opportunities. I even hear that some lenders are giving up on the pretend-and-extend and are kind of taking things to a more logical conclusion," Park said. More opportunity is set to come down the pipeline as billions of dollars worth of loans come due. Bisnow/Jon Banister Bernkopf Goodman's April DaSuta, Berkeley Garbe's Young Park and Cambridge Savings Bank's Ian Brandon From this month through the end of next year, $78B of CMBS loans are reaching their hard maturity, meaning borrowers have no extension options remaining, according to Trepp . The office sector has the most CMBS hard maturities next year, at $7.7B. Cambridge Savings Bank Executive Vice President Ian Brandon said next year's wave of loan maturities will "present a great deal of opportunity." "I'm going to feel some pain as a result," the lender said. "But I think it's something that, in many ways, is going to be a good thing in the long term for the markets." Of the buyers hunting deals now, there has been a lot of demand from foreign investors. These buyers accounted for 17% of the year-to-date investment volume among top U.S. markets, according to Avison Young. "We're seeing the biggest demand is definitely from the international market," Pepoli said. "I mean, the majority of our equity is coming into the U.S., and it's because they're taking that higher-altitude look." Pepoli said these international investors are more willing to bet on Boston because they are looking at the long-term fundamentals and aren't as focused on the near-term political issues that might keep other investors away. He said he is also seeing more "smaller shops" like his going after distressed or semidistressed deals right now. North Colony Asset Management has acquired at least three office buildings over the last year, including a 251K SF office building at 10-20 Channel Center St. in January for $52M. The deal is substantially less than the $119M LaSalle Investment Management bought it for in 2016. Pepoli said the real recovery will occur when institutional investors become more willing to buy older office buildings that have been repositioned — helping drive up prices and creating profits for the smaller players investing in upgrades. While institutions are now willing to buy top-tier office buildings like One Marina Park Drive , which Oxford Properties paid $435M for in August, he said they still haven’t been active in the Class-B segment. "Until the institutions start getting their feet wet again in there, there isn't really a huge exit market for when you've executed on these business plans," he said. See more photos from Bisnow's Boston State of the Market event below. items.title: Shadow loan fraud: The post-close risk servicers can't see
items.description: Shadow loan fraud: The post-close risk servicers can't see By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 29, 2026, 4:59 p.m. EDT 9 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email When a title insurance policy is obtained by the lender or borrower, the items which are covered are only until the time of the search. Processing Content But many deceptions involving title affect ownership of the property, including what Default Analytics describes as shadow loan fraud; these occur after the loan closes and also out of the view of the servicer . What shadow loan fraud is This form of deceit takes place "outside of the main vision of the people that are looking for it," said John Boyd, the founding principal of Default Analytics. John Boyd is the founding principal of Default Analytics It is the kind of deception that isn't seen by the originator through to the investor, he said, adding "It's really a danger that they're not even aware that lurks out there, kind of lurking in the shadows." In a normal property transaction, the buyer acquires the property with a note along with a mortgage or a deed of trust , creating the financial obligation. Most mortgage contracts have a due-on-sale clause; this can apply for other reasons as well, including the transfer of the title, Boyd said. "What happens is the property owner transfers the deed, but doesn't bother to satisfy the corresponding note and mortgage, either with the lender's consent or without," Boyd said. An assumption of the mortgage can be a "sub two," or "subject to," transaction, he said, meaning the buyer takes title while the seller's existing loan stays in place. "But an assumption is done on the premise that the lender has knowledge. A sub two is specifically structured that way, so that the lender does not have knowledge and is not directly notified of that transfer." Bill Corbet, managing director of Blackfin Group's strategic consulting practice (Blackfin has a business relationship with Default Analytics), added the servicing ecosystem works on the premise the borrower and the property owner are one and the same, and have the same interests. Those could diverge with shadow loan fraud. Why it is spreading? Today, social media posters, particularly on YouTube, are "aggressively promoting how to acquire properties without engaging the existing lender," Corbet said. Viewers are asking if such tactics are legal and the posters tend to skirt around actually answering the question, he continued. "That's something very different than what we've seen before in the industry," Corbet said. "There are always creative bad actors out there, but now with social media, their ideas are getting spread literally to hundreds of thousands of people." "Where we find ourselves now is with a lot of — we'll call it — nefarious activity going on, where individuals are coaching persons on how to acquire properties in creative ways," said industry compliance attorney John Levonick , who is also a member of the Default Analytics board of directors. Social media is helping spread the word. People are learning how to convert an owner-occupied mortgage to an investment property, the title is transferred to a business and the noteholder is not aware of the change. Why the industry has looked away Sub two fraud historically has been "somewhat ignored," Boyd said, with the attitude being as long as the payments are being made, no one is being hurt. "The movement of title has been an issue that the industry has dealt with over the years," Levonick said. But in situations where the loan continues to get paid off after the title transfer, the industry has historically turned a blind eye because in a lot of cases it is an innocuous situation and the response has been "no big harm, no big foul," he said. It typically happens when the property is placed in a living trust. Boyd noted some sub two transactions have legit motivations behind them and everything works out fine and all parties benefit. But when things go wrong, it becomes problematic. "That's not the case," he said. "It damages the whole ecosystem when these transactions transpire." For most lenders, title is the thing they look least at because they trust that the title insurer and the policy will take care of the situation if something like an unrecorded lien is found. "I'm not disparaging title companies, I think they do a really important job," said Suzy Lindblom, managing director, national operations and credit at Acra Lending, who is also a member of the Default Analytics advisory council. But I do think it's a lender's responsibility to look at that title, and I honestly think that is the least that people look at." What it costs servicers and lenders The ultimate ding for the servicer is having to write the entire loan off because of this fraud. For seller/servicers, Levonick pointed out that "an innocuous change" in who is on the title can trigger an investor repurchase demand under standard contractual terms. A concern for servicers is these non-monetary ownership changes are also inflating the property's valuation, Lindblom said. Many of these transfers are using a limited liability company to also obfuscate the ownership. "It's transferred from one LLC to another, and these LLCs typically have the same partners," Lindblom said. "Most lenders, when they lend to an LLC, anybody that has 25% or more ownership in that LLC has [provided a] personal guarantee," Lindblom said. "So you see these percentages change by LLC, but they could all be owned by the same people." Having LLC investors makes it easier for the fraudsters to hide, because those looking for it are not seeing common names, but rather anonymous entities, she said. "You kind of start into the swamp, thinking it's not going to be nearly as wide or as deep as it is," Boyd said. The wider title-fraud picture Shadow loan fraud is among a number of s

items.title: Biggest US homebuilder misses estimates, sees fewer closings
items.description: Biggest US homebuilder misses estimates, sees fewer closings By Dina Katgara Published October 29, 2026, 4:12 p.m. EDT 1 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email D.R. Horton Inc., the biggest US homebuilder, reported earnings that missed analyst estimates and said it expects to keep offering more discounts than usual to entice sluggish buyers. Processing Content The company reported earnings per share of $2.67 in the fourth quarter, below the average analyst estimate of $3.02 compiled by Bloomberg. D.R. Horton now expects to close fewer home sales in the coming fiscal year, forecasting as few as 79,000 closings in 2027 compared to about 84,000 this year. Rising rates, affordability constraints and cautious consumer sentiment pressured demand in the quarter, Executive Chairman David Auld said in a statement. READ MORE: DR Horton fights RICO suit over lowballed escrow estimates "There's just a lot of noise today out there," Chief Executive Officer Paul Romanowski said in a call with analysts Thursday. "It would be nice to go through a spring without an additional shock or something coming out there so that people can settle down" and buy homes, he said. D.R. Horton focuses on entry-level buyers sensitive to borrowing cost changes. Romanowski said expecting rates to fall is "imprudent," but added that greater geopolitical stability, lower gas prices and stronger consumer confidence could help the housing market. In the meantime, homebuilders are using a variety of discounts or sweeteners to help sell houses when demand weakens. The so-called incentives — things like providing below-market mortgage rates and reducing closing costs — cut into profit margins. More than half of builders reported using sales incentives in October, according to the National Association of Home Builders. READ MORE: ADU project volume, cost growth an opportunity for lenders D.R. Horton said it expects its use of incentives to remain higher into the new fiscal year. The company's shares rose as much as 2.2% in New York trading Thursday. Dina Katgara Bloomberg News

items.title: Zillow OKs $212 million settlement in suit over iBuying failure
items.description: Zillow OKs $212 million settlement in suit over iBuying failure By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published October 29, 2026, 3:47 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: See why Zillow agreed to a $212.5 million settlement over its defunct homebuying program. Supporting Data: By the third quarter of 2021, the iBuying unit had to sell off 7,000 homes, and cost Zillow hundreds of millions of dollars in writedowns. Zillow is paying a whopping settlement to get rid of a class action lawsuit over the demise of its massive iBuyer program earlier this decade. The real estate giant said Wednesday it agreed to a $212.5 million deal to resolve a longstanding class action lawsuit accusing the firm of misleading investors about the performance of Zillow Offers . The settlement is one of the largest payouts in the industry in recent years , and is a costly coda for a homebuying initiative that collapsed during the refinance boom. Processing Content The Zillow Offers program was created in 2018, and was responsible for up to 70% of purchase leads for the company's Zillow Home Loans origination arm. The company in 2021 ramped up its homebuying efforts in a bid to capture market share, but ended up overpaying for thousands of homes in a major misstep. Plaintiffs sued Zillow and its executive leadership for allegedly making false and misleading statements about the unit's performance throughout 2021, despite the company's scrambling behind the scenes. Executives eventually blamed the company's pricing algorithm it had previously touted. In reaching the settlement, Zillow denied wrongdoing. A spokesperson for the company said Zillow was pleased to reach a resolution, while attorneys for plaintiffs didn't respond to requests for comment Thursday. The number of class members, nor attorney's awards, weren't disclosed this week. Why Zillow Offers failed The program helped power Zillow's origination machine to over $1 billion in origination volume by the third quarter of 2021. During that time, the company embarked on a fated effort to catch up to iBuyer rival Opendoor and ramped up its home purchases, offering prices above what its algorithms suggested, the suit said. Whereas the company bought 1,856 homes in the first quarter of 2021, it rapidly increased those purchases to 9,680 in the third quarter alone. At the same time, Zillow also decreased the scope of its home renovations and the prices it paid to contractors, hoping to present sellers with higher financial offers and save costs. Employees began to raise red flags about the home purchasing activity, according to the lawsuit and other media reports, and contractors began to decline work on the Zillow homes. The unit lost Zillow more than $380 million in the third quarter. By November 2021, Zillow was looking to sell off 7,000 homes, and reported massive nine-figure inventory writedowns in the second half of 2021. Zillow closed the Offers program in November 2021, blaming its pricing algorithms, labor issues, and its renovation backlog. Next steps Of the settlement amount, $48 million will be covered by insurance, Zillow noted in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The class includes all persons who bought Zillow Class A or Class C stock between Aug. 5, 2021 and Nov. 2, 2021. Both of those stocks lost approximately 41% of their value during that stretch, with the Class A stock falling from a high of $112.50 per share to $65.86 per share by Nov. 3. The Seattle-based business faces a few other class action lawsuits, including a case alleging the firm steered borrowers to its originations arm. The company has denied those accusations. Zillow Home Loans meanwhile has chugged along, posting larger revenue and origination gains in its most recent period. For the second quarter, Zillow reported $84 million in mortgage segment revenue and $2.2 billion in purchase loan volume, both up significantly quarterly and annually. items.title: Freddie Mac's loan acquisitions top Fannie's as rates rise
items.description: Freddie Mac's loan acquisitions top Fannie's as rates rise By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 29, 2026, 3:27 p.m. EDT 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: See why Freddie Mac's new loan acquisitions moved ahead of Fannie Mae's in the third quarter. What's at Stake: Competition between Fannie and Freddie could make them more willing to open up the credit box for lenders who sell loans to them. A profitable Freddie Mac regained its lead over larger competitor Fannie Mae in single-family loan acquisitions during the third quarter as higher rates intensified competition between them. Freddie, which is the smaller of the two government-sponsored enterprises when it comes to its outstanding portfolio size, reported Thursday that it acquired $98 billion in home mortgages during the fiscal period. Fannie Mae , in comparison, purchased $88 billion in single-family loans. Processing Content These and other numbers in their recent earnings raises the question of what Freddie is doing to capture more loan acquisitions and whether it's opening up the credit box to do it. The latest underwriting indicators in earnings show Freddie's credit score and loan-to-value ratio tolerances are slightly higher, but the growth in credit reserves and some elevated delinquency measures at both GSEs suggests both will be cautious about the size of their credit boxes. "We are growing our financial strength, applying disciplined decision-making and risk management, and continuing to invest in the capabilities that can make the housing system work better," Freddie Mac Chief Financial Officer Jim Whitlinger said in the GSE's earnings call. What underwriting indicators show Whitlinger reported that Freddie's weighted average current loan-to-value ratio was 54% and the equivalent credit score was 755 in the company's third-quarter earnings call. Fannie's equivalent credit score number was 753 and its mark-to-market loan-to-value ratio was 51%. Current or mark-to-market LTVs on the outstanding portfolios account for property value changes and paydowns on loans over time. Weighted averages for original LTVs are generally higher and have averaged more around 78%, according to Fannie. The underwriting metrics for new acquisitions are a subset of the broader portfolio numbers. Whitlinger and others have indicated there may be more caution in that part of the market because slight increases in certain delinquency buckets have been driven by newer vintages. "The year-over-year increase was primarily driven by higher serious delinquency rates for loans originated during 2022 through 2024," Whitlinger said during the call. Both Fannie and Freddie have seen some delinquencies inch up in both their single- and multifamily book, calling for broader risk management. With risk growing, Freddie had to manage a larger-than anticipated shift from a $900 million benefit for credit losses to a $800 million reserve during the quarter, analysts at BTIG noted. Fannie also recorded a shift from a benefit for credit losses to a reserve in the period. All this suggests that for the time being, Freddie and Fannie are keeping an eye on credit, which may limit how much leeway in underwriting they want to use to compete. But they still want to offer some additional support to help consumers afford homes to the extent their delinquency rates and overall financials allow. While some types of arrears are rising, the single-family serious delinquency rate is still historically low at less than 1% at both GSEs. "Financial strength matters because of what it enables us to do," Whitlinger said. "It gives us greater capacity to provide liquidity throughout the economic cycle, support sustainable homeownership and help make housing finance more efficient and affordable." Examples include a lender option that both GSEs now offer to use the modernized VantageScore 4.0 credit metric for loan pricing, which some mortgage companies have said helped them get certain borrowers approved. This was used for 6% of the loans Fredddie bought in the third quarter, Whitlinger said. Other key financial metrics to watch The GSEs so far have shown that they are financially strong from a net income perspective and have sustained the long run of profitability that followed their 2008 move into conservatorship. So long as that financial strength persists, they might do more to expand some underwriting selectively with offsetting, more conservative adjustments in other areas in line with the trend seen in the condo market. Freddie reported that quarterly net income rose by around 17% on the year to $3.2 billion, and Fannie announced a day earlier that its strongest net revenues since 2023 drove an 8% increase during the same period to $4.2 billion. The smaller GSE's $3.2 billion in growth for the quarter also brought its total net worth to $81 billion, helping to close a regulatory capital gap that's also essential to their financial soundness and an eventual conservatorship exit. Fannie also reported improvement in this area. "Excluding buffers, our capital shortfall was $98 billion at the end of third quarter 2026, largely because the $73 billion of senior preferred stock does not qualify," Whitlinger said in a reminder that an exit would need to address this, a key point prominent GSE investors have emphasized. Adjusted for the SPS, this means capital is around $21 billion below its statutory minimum level, Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analysts noted in a report on Freddie's earnings. "FMCC's capital remains subordinate to the government's senior preferred shares and liquidation preference, so any privatization would have to include either forgiveness or conversion," the KBW analysts wrote. items.title: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month
items.description: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Oct 29, 2026 Highlights In 2026Q3, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County registered at $2,554,—down $96, or 3.6%, from a year earlier. The median asking rent for 0-2 bedrooms in L.A. County was $2,239, reflecting a decline of $88 (-3.8%) from the previous year. Meanwhile, rent for 3+ bedroom units dropped by $70 (-1.9%) compared to 2025Q3, standing at $3,571. For renters in L.A. County : Buying costs far more than renting. In 2026Q3, a median-priced home cost $4,716 more a month than renting one, nearly 185% higher, even though the monthly buying cost fell about 2% as home prices dropped. Mortgage rates above 7% could erase that relief. At 7%, the same home would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the savings from lower prices In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for all rental properties listed on Realtor.com in Los Angeles County was $2,554, a decline of $96, or 3.6%, compared with a year ago. While the county experienced a temporary dip in rents during the pandemic, asking rents quickly rebounded to pre-pandemic levels and peaked in the summer of 2022. Since then, a surge in new multifamily construction has put sustained downward pressure on rent. In the most recent quarter, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County was $340, or 11.7%, below its 2022 peak. In addition, Los Angeles County renters are overwhelmingly local. In the third quarter of 2026, more than half (61.3%) of online traffic to L.A. County rental listings originated from within the county, with an additional 15.5% coming from elsewhere in California. Out-of-state renters accounted for 19.8% of traffic, while international traffic represented 3.4%. Breaking down by bedroom type, the median asking rent for 0-2 bedroom units in Los Angeles County was $2,239 in 2026Q3, a decline of $88 or 3.8%, from a year ago. Larger units with three or more bedrooms saw a comparatively modest softening, with a median asking rent of $3,571 — down $70, or 1.9%, year-over-year. The steeper rent decline among smaller units suggests renters in that segment are experiencing greater pricing relief. The surge in ADUs across Los Angeles County may partially explain this trend. As those permitted units complete construction — typically requiring 6 to 18 months from permit to occupancy — a growing wave of new small rental units has been entering the market, adding downward price pressure concentrated in the smaller unit segment. Figure 1: Rents by Unit Size in L.A. County—2026Q3 Table 1: L.A. County Rents by Unit Size, 2026Q3 Unit Size Median Asking Rent Rent YoY vs. Peak Overall $2,554 -3.6% -11.7% 0-2 beds $2,239 -3.8% -14.7% 3+ beds $3,571 -1.9% -11.3% City of Los Angeles: Relief from the peak, but still out of reach for many In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for rental properties listed on Realtor.com in the City of Los Angeles was $2,708, reflecting a decline of $92, or 3.3%, from a year earlier. Consistent with the broader L.A. County trend, rents in the City of Los Angeles have been on a downward trajectory since peaking in the summer of 2022. While the current median remains $158, or 5.5%, above pre-pandemic levels, renters today are saving $363 per month, or 11.8%, compared to the 2022 peak, translating to $4,356 in annual savings. Nevertheless, in order to afford a typical home in the city of Los Angeles, a minimum annual income of $108,320 is required— 22.1% higher than the city's estimated median household income of $88,730 1 High mortgage rates squeeze renters hoping to buy Renters may be catching a break, but for most renters who want to become homeowners in L.A. County, homeownership remains out of reach. On top of that, with mortgage rates now above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push homeownership even further out of reach for renters who want to buy. In 2026Q3, buying a typical home in L.A. County costs $4,716 more per month than renting one. Buying got slightly cheaper over the past year because home prices fell, even as mortgage rates rose. The median listing price dropped 3.2% to $970,000 over the past year, which more than offset a small increase in the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, from 6.57% to 6.68%. As a result, the estimated monthly cost of buying a median-priced home fell about 2.1%, or $159, from a year earlier, to $7,270. But that relief may not last. Rates surpassed 7% in late-September and remain well- above this mark. At 7%, the same home price would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the monthly payment savings from lower prices. Methodology To determine the monthly cost of buying a home, we find the median listing price for homes in Los Angeles County. As first-time homebuyers plan lower down payments, we assume a 10% down payment and use the 30-year fixed mortgage rate during the quarter to calculate a monthly mortgage payment. We also include the HOA fees, taxes, and homeowners insurance as part of the costs. L.A. rental data as of 2026Q3 for all units advertised for rent on Realtor.com®. Rental units include apartments as well as private rentals (condos, townhomes, single-family homes). We use rental sources that reliably report data each month within L.A. county. To calculate the median asking rent for each quarter, we first obtain the median asking rent for each month within that quarter and then take the average of the three months. Footnotes Data Source: Claritas’ estimation based on Census ACS data.

items.title: Luxury Cut: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking
items.description: Luxury Cut: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking By Anthony Smith Oct 29, 2026 The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking St Louis Downtown and Arch – SeanPavonePhoto/Adobe Stock St. Louis Returns to the Top St. Louis has made its way back to the top spot this quarter in the Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking. The top 5 rounds out with Charlottesville, VA; Portland, ME; Bridgeport, CT; and Pittsfield, MA, which took the top spot last quarter. Common themes across the top-ranked markets include low climate risk, lower unemployment rates, and higher levels of buyer demand. Each quarter, Realtor.com and the Wall Street Journal team up to identify the highest-performing and most attractive metro areas for luxury home purchases. We score 60 different luxury housing markets across the country in categories that include supply and demand strength, economic health, and quality of life. This fall’s ranking points to a return to fundamentals: markets with active buyer demand, homes that sell at a steady pace, and low exposure to climate risk moved to the front of the pack, while several lifestyle-driven markets that led earlier this year slipped out of the top 10. Highlights St. Louis climbs from No. 12 to No. 1 , reclaiming the top spot it last held in summer 2025, backed by the lowest cost of living in the ranking, strong buyer demand, and minimal climate risk. Four new entries joined the top 10 : St. Louis, Portland, ME (No. 3), Bridgeport, CT (No. 4), and Detroit (No. 6). Charlottesville, VA, reaches No. 2 , its highest placement yet, extending its run to six straight quarters in the top 10. Four markets exited the top 10 . Boulder, CO, fell from No. 2 to No. 15. San Jose, CA, dropped from No. 3 to No. 37. Santa Fe, NM, slipped from No. 4 to No. 16, and Santa Barbara, CA, moved from No. 10 to No. 17. items.title: Beloved ‘Star Trek’ Actor Patrick Stewart Dies at Home in Los Angeles
items.description: Actor Patrick Stewart , celebrated for his legendary roles in "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and all five "X-Men" movies, died in his Los Angeles, CA home on Wednesday, Oct. 28 at the age of 86. "We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," an Oct. 29 Instagram post shared to Stewart's account reads. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayers, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," the statement continued. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace." A Yorkshire, England native, Stewart split his time between his homes in California , Park Slope, Brooklyn , and the United Kingdom. In a 2014 discussion with Vanity Fair , he explained that he had always dreamt of moving to the United States, having seen aspirational American homes on screen. Loading... Legendary "Star Trek" actor Patrick Stewart has passed away in his Los Angeles home at the age of 86. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images Loading... The Yorkshire native split his time between his homes in California, New York, and the United Kingdom. Paul Harris/Getty Images "The movies were my passion when I was a child," he explained, noting that he didn't own a television until he was 26 years old. "I loved movies about American life. I was growing up in a working-class neighborhood in a very small house, and I loved movies about American homes with green lawns and beautiful, big kitchens, and so it was the glamour of American life as it was portrayed in the movies." Eventually, it was a film called "On the Waterfront" that introduced Stewart to Red Hook, Brooklyn, a location he'd later live just "a block away from." "I saw that movies could be about something other than pure escapism and fantasy," he said, noting that the film was "actually about the kind of people" that he was used to spending time around as a child. Brooklyn was also the place where Stewart met his wife, Sunny Ozell , 47, in 2008. "She was working as a waitress in a restaurant in Brooklyn," Stewart told People magazine of the chance encounter. "This lovely woman came over and said, 'Gentlemen, on the house, what would you like for desserts?'" As the pair got to talking, Stewart—who was starring in a Brooklyn Academy of Music production of "Macbeth" at the time—learned Ozell had been hoping to see the show, but was disappointed that the limited run had been sold out before opening. He gave Ozell his phone number, and promised to secure her a ticket. "And that's what we did," he shared. "And she came backstage afterward and we had dinner and here we are." The couple married in 2013, residing in a Park Slope duplex penthouse the actor purchased for $2.5 million the year prior, according to Business Insider. The 2,176-square-foot home boasted 11-foot ceilings and a converted carriage house. A year later, Stewart explained that he and Ozell had fully embraced a Brooklyn lifestyle—jokingly citing the amount of kale that they ate at the time, and quipping that he was planning on "beginning a campaign" to ban "strollers from sidewalks." In the same interview, Stewart revealed he was planning to spend "a large part of the summer" in his home in "a very pretty part of the U.K." Although Stewart would later offload the idyllic Yorkshire Dales home he was referring to in 2016, the decision to reside in two countries was an intentional move to stay connected to his roots. "I was fearful of losing myself to Hollywood in the way I'd seen other British stage actors do," he told The Yorkshire Post after selling his home. "I wanted a toehold in England, somewhere to come home to." In 2019, Stewart purchased the former home of "Modern Family" director Jason Winer—a 4,500-square-foot Los Angeles estate he snapped up for $4.3 million, according to Yahoo! Finance . items.title: MLB Legend Matt Holliday Lists Stunning Arizona Estate for $11.6M Just Months After Buying It
items.description: Retired Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday is ready to part ways with the newly built Paradise Valley, AZ , estate he purchased earlier this year. The World Series champion —who previously played for the New York Yankees , Colorado Rockies , Oakland Athletics , and St. Louis Cardinals —has listed his five-bedroom, six-bedroom abode for $11.6 million after snapping it up for $10.6 million in February, according to records. A respiratory disease led Holliday, 46 and his wife, Leslee Holliday , 47 to leave their former home in Stillwater, OK , listing agent Vincent Clark of VCRE told the Phoenix Business Journal . “The doctor said he needed to get to dry climate quick,” said Clark, who noted that Holliday had received the diagnosis after a water leak affected their 136-acre dream home, which is still on the market. The listing indicates “the residence received substantial healthy-home enhancements” following an “extensive” assessment. Updates include air and water filtration and conditioning systems, and a dedicated multistage reverse-osmosis drinking system. Loading... Retired MLB star Matt Holliday has listed his Paradise Valley estate for $11.6 million, less than a year after snapping it up for $10.6 million. Rocket Lister Loading... Holliday initially relocated to Arizona from Oklahoma after receiving doctors' orders to "get to dry climate quick" after receiving a respiratory disease diagnosis, said listing agent Vincent Clark. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Loading... The sprawling estate includes a resortlike outdoor space with a 60-foot lap pool. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Loading... The Hollidays are reportedly hoping to find a home with an existing guesthouse, while the Paradise Valley property has approved plans for a casita. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Additional updates include Control4 automation—a smart home program that “integrates the residence.” The property includes transferred approved plans for an 845-square-foot guest casita, but according to Clark, the Hollidays are seeking a home with an existing guesthouse. However, the home does include a generously-sized guest suite. Situated on a lot just over an acre, the 7,781-square-foot home was built in 2025. Its contemporary design is defined by glass walls boasting breathtaking views of Camelback Mountain, as the surrounding landscape creates a serene environment in every inch of the home. The outdoor area features 3,000 square feet of covered space and stunning resort-style landscaping. Loading... Unobstructed views of Camelback Mountain are available from the primary suite. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Loading... The spa-worthy primary bathroom includes a double vanity and sky-high ceilings. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Loading... A soaking tub and a sizable walk-in shower add to the peaceful vibe of the room. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Loading... The contemporary home was built in 2025. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ Loading... The property boasts an office, a recreation or theater room, and a flexible fitness space. Casey Rae Barnabas/SunRae Media AZ A 60-foot lap pool includes a heated spa, and the area is perfectly primed for entertaining with multiple fire features, a built-in barbecue, and lots of space to lounge. Inside, a modern, open-concept floor plan adds to the tranquil vibe of the estate. The great room is truly remarkable, with a dramatic 14-foot multislide door that provides direct access to the palm tree-lined courtyard oasis. The kitchen has multiple ovens, a sizable walk-in pantry, and a large island with plenty of storage and room to dine. Unobstructed mountain views set the tone in the sprawling primary suite, which includes a spa-worthy bathroom featuring a double vanity and sky-high ceilings. Three of the additional bedrooms also include en suite bathrooms. Decorated with funky green wallpaper, the office is an inspiring corner of the home. There’s also a space to be used as a recreation or theater room, and a flexible fitness space for those who prefer to exercise without having to leave the house. The climate-controlled garage is a major perk in the Arizona heat, and has room for four cars. Loading... The Hollidays previously lived in a 136-acre Oklahoma estate, which is still on the market for $8.95 million. Wyatt Poindexter - The Agency Loading... The baseball field has professional lighting and turf. Wyatt Poindexter - The Agency Loading... The list of amenities is impressive and includes indoor pickleball and basketball courts. Wyatt Poindexter - The Agency Although it sits on a smaller parcel of land, the Paradise Valley home is comparable in size to the 7,500-square-foot Oklahoma abode the Hollidays are still trying to sell, although the latter features many more customizations. From Gucci wallpaper to a $2 million two-level pool with a luxury hot tub and a fully equipped outdoor kitchen, the family’s former property spares no expense. The host of amenities is jaw-dropping and includes a professionally lit baseball field, indoor pickleball and basketball courts, and a guesthouse. "One of the things I've loved most about this home is the opportunity it has given us to gather people together," Holliday shared in a statement to Mansion Global. "Some of our favorite memories here revolve around hosting college students and professional athletes for meals, conversation, and meaningful fellowship." Still, it struggles to find a buyer, and has taken two price slashes since originally hitting the market for $12 million in February 2026. In May, it was discounted to $9.8 million before dropping down to $8.95 million in September. An estimated $3 million worth of custom furniture has been included in the listing to sweeten the deal, which can also include additional land. items.title: Passengers Who Sold Their Homes for a $120K ‘Perpetual Cruise’ Are Now Stranded in Cambodia
items.description: Randy Cassingham thought he was embarking on the adventure of a lifetime—a never-ending cruise that would take him around the world and across multiple continents. That was the promise of Villa Vie Residences’ Odyssey cruise, set to visit 147 countries and 425 ports over a period of 3.5 years. Passengers had three options: They could rent a villa through the Odyssey’s “rent-to-own” program starting at $3,499 a month, which allowed passengers to join the cruise at any point along the way. Or they could purchase a five-year residency on the cruise ship starting at $59,999. The final option was a permanent residency—good for the life of the cruise ship—which started at $119,999, with villa suites going for as much as $439,999. Villa Vie is still advertising these cabins as available on its website. Cassingham was among many passengers who sold their belongings—including their homes—for the chance to live aboard a cruise ship for the rest of his life. “We were planning on being on for, you know, forever,” Cassingham told the Times Radio . “They were guaranteeing that this ship would last 15 years and I think it was in good enough shape that it could have. And that was our plan. We were going to stay there until we decided we didn't want to do it anymore or we died. One or the other.” But just two years on, Cassingham’s “never-ending cruise” came to an abrupt end. Earlier this week, Villa Vie told the 200 or so passengers aboard the Odyssey that they would have to disembark in Cambodia because the company could no longer afford to run the ship. Villa Vie said the culprit was the rising cost of fuel due to the war in Iran and repeated closures of the Strait of Hormuz. According to Villa Vie’s estimates, per-cabin fuel expenses rose from $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 per month, putting “its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure.” “Since the conflict [in Iran] began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company’s statement continued. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.” It also probably didn't help that the 650-capacity ship was never fully booked. Villa Vie said on its website that the Odyssey was 85% sold, but Cassingham said he believed that the ship topped out at around 350 passengers. Residents said they had been aware of ongoing financial issues. Pamela Reckamp told NBC News that at a September meeting, ship officials asked residents to help raise $1 million so they could refuel the ship in Vietnam. Loading... A passenger walks through the empty Odyssey cruise ship after travelers on the ship were asked to disembark in Cambodia because the ship ran out of fuel. TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images On Monday morning, passengers heard an announcement coming over the loudspeaker: “Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations. As a result, the Odyssey will officially enter a ‘temporary layup’ this afternoon. All residents must disembark by 2 p.m. today.” In a press release, Villa Vie said it would be “working to support those affected as plans develop.” However, a blog post on Cassingham’s website, Residential Cruising , contradicted that. “The company has done absolutely nothing to help,” he wrote. “We couldn’t even walk out of the port, so there were shuttle buses that dropped us in the middle of town, Sihanoukville, Cambodia, the end. They didn’t even give us a list of hotels, let alone help us get there or pay for them.” That left Cassingham and many other passengers bewildered about what to do next. “We had built a house, and it was our dream house, and we decided to sell that and our cars and almost all of our belongings and move onto the ship full-time permanently,” he told Radio Times. “We don't have a home to go to right now. We don't know what we're going to do exactly.” Realtor.com® has reached out to Villa Vie Residences for comment. Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

items.title: Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
items.description:
Earnings Press Release
Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
Dallas, TX, October 28, 2026 — Invitation Homes Inc. (NYSE: INVH) (“Invitation Homes,” “we,” “our,” and “us”), the nation’s
premier single-family home leasing and management company, today announced our Third Quarter (“Q3”) 2026 financial and
operating results.


Q3 2026 Highlights
•   Year over year, total revenues increased 6.3% to $731 million, property operating and maintenance costs increased 2.0% to
    $264 million, and net income available to common stockholders increased 15.6% to $158 million, or $0.27 per diluted
    common share.
•   Year over year, Core FFO per share increased 2.4% to $0.48, while AFFO per share increased 0.1% to $0.38.
•   Same Store NOI increased 1.1% year over year on 1.6% Same Store Core Revenues growth and 2.5% Same Store Core
    Operating Expenses growth.
•   Same Store Average Occupancy was 96.4%, a reduction of 10 basis points year over year.
•   Same Store renewal rent growth of 4.3% and Same Store new lease rent growth of (0.2)% resulted in Same Store blended
    rent growth of 3.0%.
•   We sold 658 wholly owned homes, most to families purchasing for their own use, and acquired 216 wholly owned homes,
    for net dispositions of 442 homes and net proceeds of approximately $245 million that we used to fund share repurchases.
•   As previously announced, on July 8, 2026, we closed a public offering of $500 million aggregate principal amount of 4.950%
    senior notes (the “Notes”). The Notes were priced at 99.291% of the principal amount and mature on February 1, 2032. Net
    proceeds were used to prepay a portion of our secured debt obligation maturing in June 2027.


Capital Allocation Update
From December 1, 2025 through October 27, 2026, we bought back nearly $1 billion of our shares. This includes an aggregate
of 36,923,753 shares repurchased to date at an average stock price of $26.78, and represents an implied value per home of
approximately $280,000 against a gross average sales price of approximately $460,000 for homes sold during that same period.


On October 26, 2026, our board of directors authorized an additional $500 million share repurchase program.


Comments from Chief Executive Officer Dallas Tanner
“Our third quarter reflected steady execution across the platform. Same Store NOI grew 1.1% year over year, blended rent growth
was 3.0%, and with the benefit of our share repurchases, Core FFO per share grew 2.4%. Since December 2025, we’ve
repurchased nearly $1 billion of our stock at a substantial valuation discount. We believe that is more than any other residential
REIT. With the new $500 million share repurchase program our board just authorized, we intend to keep funding buybacks with
home sale proceeds whenever our stock trades at a meaningful discount to the value of our homes, guided by market conditions
and a disciplined approach to the balance sheet.”


“Following a solid third quarter, we are raising our full year guidance midpoints for Core FFO per share by $0.01 to $1.96, Same
Store NOI growth guidance to 1.2%, and wholly owned home sales to $950 million, which supports our continued focus on
closing the gap between public and private market values.”
 Glossary & Reconciliations of Non-GAAP Financial and Other Operating Measures
Financial and operating measures found in the Earnings Release and Supplemental Information include certain measures used by
Invitation Homes management that are measures not defined under accounting principles generally accepted in the United States
(“GAAP”). These measures are defined herein and, as applicable, reconciled to the most comparable GAAP measures.
Financial Results

Net Income
Net income per common share — diluted for Q3 2026 was $0.27, compared to net income per common share — diluted of $0.22
for Q3 2025. Total revenues and total property operating and maintenance expenses for Q3 2026 were $731 million and $264
million, respectively, compared to $688 million and $259 million, respectively, for Q3 2025.


Net income per common share — diluted for YTD 2026 was $0.90, compared to net income per share — diluted of $0.72 for
YTD 2025. Total revenues and total property operating and maintenance expenses for YTD 2026 were $2,213 million and
$771 million, respectively, compared to $2,044 million and $741 million, respectively, for YTD 2025.


Core FFO
Year over year, Core FFO per share for Q3 2026 increased 2.4% to $0.48, while Core FFO per share for YTD 2026 increased
2.1% to $1.46, primarily due to a lower share count from stock repurchases and Same Store NOI growth.


AFFO
Year over year, AFFO per share for Q3 2026 increased 0.1% to $0.38, while AFFO per share for YTD 2026 increased 1.1% to
$1.23, primarily due to the increase in Core FFO per share described above.

items.title: Mortgage Rates
items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 10/29/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.24% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.60% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline Further to 7.24% The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.24% as of October 29, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.32%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.17%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.60%, down from last week when it averaged 6.68%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: U.S. Retail Demand Remains Solid as Limited Construction Keeps Space Tight
items.description: U.S. Retail Demand Remains Solid as Limited Construction Keeps Space Tight Phoebe Schmidt • 10/29/2026 Q3 U.S. Retail Marketbeat Shopping centers recorded 3.5 million square feet of net absorption in Q3, with fitness, wellness and value retailers leading leasing activity New York -- U.S. shopping center demand remained solid in the third quarter of 2026 as retailers backfilled vacated stores and selectively expanded their footprints, according to Cushman & Wakefield's latest U.S. Retail MarketBeat report . Limited construction continued to support market fundamentals, with national vacancy holding steady at 5.9%, well below the historical average of 7.4%. Net absorption totaled 3.5 million square feet in Q3, the second-strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2023, bringing year-to-date absorption into positive territory at 1.2 million square feet. The improvement followed first-half declines that reflected seasonal weakness and the effects of store closures in 2025. "Retail demand has remained solid beneath the quarterly fluctuations," said James Bohnaker , Principal Economist at Cushman & Wakefield. "Retailers are backfilling space left by earlier closures and continuing to expand selectively. For tenants looking to grow, finding the right space in a quality shopping center remains a challenge." Fitness, wellness and value-oriented retailers are leading categories for leasing activity, reflecting a continued shift toward consumer services and demand for affordable shopping options. Discount retailers accounted for 1,046 store openings year to date, while off-price apparel retailers added 214 locations. New construction remained limited, with just 2.3 million square feet delivered during the quarter. The development pipeline represented only 0.4% of existing inventory. National asking rents reached $25.80 per square foot, up 2.2% year over year, although the pace of growth moderated. "With so little new space being built, even modest expansion can keep availability tight," Bohnaker said. "Consumer spending is holding steady, but retailers remain disciplined about where they open stores. Well-located centers with strong tenant mixes are best positioned to capture that demand." Demand was positive across several regions. The West absorbed 1.4 million square feet and remained the only region to record positive absorption in every quarter of 2026, led in Q3 by Phoenix, the Inland Empire and Orange County. The Northeast recorded 1.2 million square feet of absorption, with vacancy declining in eight of its 11 tracked markets. The Midwest led regional asking rent growth at 3.6% year over year, with Columbus, Cincinnati and St. Louis among the strongest-performing markets nationally. The South accounted for 52% of year-to-date construction completions but maintained the lowest regional vacancy rate at 5.7%. Cushman & Wakefield expects retail fundamentals to remain resilient through year-end, supported by limited new supply and continued tenant demand. Performance will vary by market and property, with location, tenant quality and retailers' value propositions remaining key differentiators. Cushman & Wakefield's quarterly retail report can be found here . Despite ongoing occupancy hurdles, leasing activity remained relatively active with nearly 1.4 msf transacted YTD. Total nonfarm employment declined 1.7% to just over 1.2 million jobs, while the Portland unemployment held steady year-over-year – at 5.0%, it remained 80 basis points higher than the national rate of 4.2%. Looking ahead, while employment growth is expected to remain muted, relatively stable labor market conditions should support a gradual recovery in office leasing activity as occupiers gain greater confidence in long-term space planning. Supply and Demand: Market Continues to Rebalance The Portland office market continued to navigate challenging demand conditions during the third quarter, as occupiers remained selective and continued to prioritize efficiency in their space requirements. Overall vacancy rose to 23.9%, while quarterly net absorption was minimally negative at 21,000 square feet (sf), bringing year-to-date absorption to negative 627,000 sf. Despite ongoing occupancy hurdles, leasing activity remained relatively active with nearly 1.4 million square feet transacted year-to-date. items.description: Share: Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn I recommend visiting cushmanwakefield.com to read:%0A%0A {0} %0A%0A {1} Insights Miami Retail MarketBeat This MarketBeat report covers the Miami retail real estate market for Q3 2026, highlighting key themes across supply, demand, pricing, and retail sales activity. Read the report for the full details and insights. DOWNLOAD THE Q3 2026 REPORT Key Takeaways Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 msf underway. Vacancy increased 10 bps QOQ to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 psf in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. Supply Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 million square feet (msf) underway. Construction commenced on nearly 63,000 square feet (sf) of new retail space during the quarter. Meanwhile, deliveries totaled 78,000 sf, bringing year-to-date (YTD) deliveries to 158,000 sf. This represented a 64.6% year-over-year (YOY) decrease from the 447,000 sf delivered during the same period in 2025. Vacancy increased 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Despite the slight increase, Miami-Dade County’s retail market continued to demonstrate tight conditions, with vacancy remaining the lowest among Florida markets, below Fort Lauderdale at 4.2%, Orlando at 3.9% and Tampa at 3.8%. Demand Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. The market recorded negative 81,000 sf of net absorption during the quarter, bringing the YTD total to negative 129,000 sf. Although occupancy losses have persisted in six of the past seven quarters, quarterly performance improved considerably from negative 230,000 sf in the third quarter of 2025. At the submarket level, Kendall and Miami Airport led occupancy gains, recording 97,000 sf and nearly 51,000 sf of positive absorption, respectively. These gains were offset by losses in Coral Gables (negative 41,000 sf) and Northeast Dade (negative 35,000 sf). By property type, malls posted the strongest performance, with occupancy gains of just under 12,000 sf, while general retail recorded the largest decline at negative 62,000 sf. Overall, leasing activity and occupancy trends remained mixed across the county, with gains in select submarkets and property types offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Looking ahead, the construction pipeline may provide additional opportunities for retailers as new space enters the market, although future occupancy gains will depend on demand keeping pace with new supply. Pricing Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 per square foot (psf) in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Among the county’s retail submarkets, Miami Beach commanded the highest average asking rent at $97.85 psf, while Miami recorded the lowest at $31.92 psf. Compared YOY, average asking rents increased in 16 submarkets and declined in three. Outlying Miami-Dade County recorded the largest YOY increase, with rents rising 4.1% from $40.97 psf to $42.65 psf. In contrast, Brickell asking rents declined 2.4% YOY to $84.96 psf. Retail Sales Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. This brought YTD transaction volume to $1.2 billion across 2.0 msf. YTD transaction volume declined 25.5% YOY and was 6.6% below the five-year average. Miami Airport led all submarkets with $265.8 million in sales. Notable transactions included the $72.0 million sale of Airpark Plaza, located at 5715 NW Seventh Street in the Miami Airport submarket. By property type, strip malls recorded the highest average sale price at $815 psf during the quarter. Pricing remained elevated, with Miami averaging $450 psf, well above the U.S. average of $246 psf, underscoring the market’s continued premium positioning. Miami-Dade County’s retail capitalization rates ranged from 4.9% to 7.2%, averaging 5.8%. This was below the national average of 7.4%, indicating that local retail properties continued to trade at lower yields than the national average. items.title: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter
items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. Report Methodology ATTOM analyzed county tax assessor data for over 105.1 million residential properties for vacancy, broken down by foreclosure status and owner-occupancy status in the fourth quarter of 2026. Only metropolitan statistical areas with at least 100,000 residential properties and 50 properties in pre-foreclosure, counties with at least 50,000 residential properties and zip codes with at least 1,000 residential properties and 25 in pre-foreclosure were included in the analysis.
