items.title: A path to sub-7% mortgage rates is back on the table
items.description: Housing demand has stabilized over the last two weeks as rates have fallen a tad, and we can finally see a clear path back to sub-7% mortgage rates . We survived the crazy month of October, when the 10-year had the potential to close above 5.35%, which would have created a backdrop of bond-escalation selling, sending mortgage rates above 8%. That didn’t happen, of course, as the 10-year yield held that key line! Not only has the 10-year yield now gone below 5% — with mortgage rates closer to 7% than 8% today — but what this month has shown us is that there’s a clear path for sub-7% mortgage rates. Just the move in the last two weeks has stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, so let’s take a look on this Halloween on what needs to happen to get rates lower. 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week was Fed week, and even Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said tighter policy has created financial pain for some AI companies. The Federal Reserve has been talking more and more about AI being very inflationary for many weeks now, so naturally, when AI companies are having debt-financing issues, and some are missing on their numbers, the 10-year yield has gone lower even with elevated oil prices and economic data staying firm. However, imagine for a minute that the Iran conflict was over: oil would be trading between $67 and $82. Imagine that the trade war 2.0 doesn’t get worse and you have an AI slowdown; there’s your trinity for lower mortgage rates. Nothing too drastic, but definitely sub-7%, and we’ve all seen what mortgage demand can do when rates drop below 6.64%. So there’s a pathway to 7%, but there’s also a pathway for rates to stay above 7% if the AI story rebounds, the conflict doesn’t end, and the trade war continues. This, of course, would need the economic data to stay very positive, as it has recently. Since Sept. 10, a clear head-and-shoulders pattern has formed in the 10-year yield so what I said above can break that lower and get us sub-7% rates. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they’re still trending near multi-year lows. I can’t stress enough how important it is for spreads to be closer to 2% than 3%, since mortgage rates would already be over 8% now if this were not the case. Not only that, it would have been impossible to get mortgage rates near 7% again without a much bigger move lower with the 10-year yield. That said, when the 10-year yield moves lower at times, spreads can widen after a big move up because their job is to compress volatility. Now, this does wear off over time, and we can head lower again. What you don’t want to see is the Fed suddenly changing course and starting a massive rate-hike cycle, or a credit event like the Silicon Valley Bank crisis. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads were flat at 2.23% from week to week. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been over the last three years, given the 10-year yield’s current level: If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.15% today, not 7.27%. If we had the worst levels of 2024, mortgage rates would be 7.77% today. If we had the worst levels of 2025, mortgage rates would be 7.58% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. The key for the last two weeks: lower rates even above 7%, have stabilized demand, as our weekly pending home sales are still higher than two weeks ago. That is all we should take from this move, and we will see how rates affect the data going forward. Rule of thumb for the last three years and 10 months: housing demand typically grows when rates are under 6.64% and heading toward 6%, and doesn’t show growth when rates are over 6.64% and heading above 7%. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 52,050 2025: 55,214 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. I expected some week-to-week growth last week, as our tracker showed growth too; we did have a 4% week-to-week gain, but it's still down significantly year over year. When rates were closer to 6%, every week except one showed year-over-year growth. items.title: Exclusive: CrossCountry Mortgage demands payment from former LOs, invokes 2-year non-solicitation
items.description: Top-five mortgage lender CrossCountry Mortgage ( CCM ) has sent cease-and-desist letters to at least 25 former loan officers, according to documents viewed by HousingWire and interviews with one of their new employers. In the letters, CCM invokes a two-year, non-solicitation window and demands thousands of dollars in combined penalties under their employment agreements. The company cites a contractual provision creating a “legal presumption” that any mortgage product or service provided to a past, present or future CCM customer violates the agreement. Under that framework, CCM declares that “each loan is presumed to violate your non-solicitation covenant.” The letters, dated Oct. 29, were sent by Ashley C. Wakefield, senior corporate counsel for Cleveland-based CrossCountry Mortgage. Each document contains the same three-part demand: a cease-and-desist order, a demand for payment based on 75 bps for each refinanced loan, and a litigation preservation notice. CCM gives the recipients 10 business days to respond. According to the letters seen by HousingWire, the repayment amounts range from several thousand dollars to nearly $20,000 dollars in the case of one letter. Representatives at CrossCountry Mortgage did not immediately respond to HousingWire ’s request for comment. Details of the claims CCM’s letters lean heavily on restrictive covenants in the employment agreements allegedly signed by the LOs. CCM argues that the agreements contain provisions around confidentiality, nonsolicitation and return of property provisions that survive an employee’s departure. The company asserts that confidential material covered by the agreements includes all non-public personal information of borrowers that is protected under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. It goes on to say that every loan handled by the LOs during their time there “remains CCM’s sole and exclusive property.” How many LOs could be impacted? While the letters obtained by HousingWire address a small number of LOs, many others have left CCM in recent years for other companies. They could be part of a larger pattern of cease-and-desist orders, along with potential litigation, if they’ve closed loans since then with any CCM customers. RETR data shows that 843 loan officers have left CrossCountry Mortgage in the past 14 months. Sixty-one of them did at least $20 million in volume during that period, although it’s unknown how much of that volume was tied to former CCM clients. Many others are now inactive LOs or have produced no loans. Beyond the cash demands — which were labeled as payable by check mailed to CCM’s headquarters in Cleveland within 10 business days — the letters call for the recipients to stop originating loans for any CCM customer, prospect or referral source, to stop using any CCM confidential material, and to certify in writing that they’ve returned all company materials. The letters also include a warning that “litigation over these matters is reasonably likely.” The recipients are instructed to preserve a sweeping range of records, including offer letters and compensation details from their current employer, along with loan files, lead-source data, CRM and loan origination system records, and communications with any current or former CCM borrower. This preservation demand also mentions personal devices and digital tools, specifically naming email, text and instant messages, voicemails, call logs, calendar entries, shared drives, cloud accounts and “AI chat history.” The recipients are instructed to immediately suspend any auto-delete or device replacement practices, warning that failure to preserve evidence “may expose you to sanctions for spoliation.” If the recipients don’t comply within 10 business days, “CCM may file suit without further notice,” the letters state. Editor's note: Sarah Wolak contributed to this report. Related More: CrossCountry Mortgage Loan Officer

items.title: Silvio Tavares steps down as VantageScore CEO, Anthony Hutchinson named interim leader
items.description: VantageScore announced on Friday that president and CEO Silvio Tavares is stepping down after five years leading the credit scoring company, with Anthony Hutchinson appointed as interim CEO. VantageScore 's board has begun a formal search for a permanent successor, according to a company release. Hutchinson, who previously led VantageScore's public affairs and government relations efforts, will work with the board and management team during the transition. The company did not specify Tavares' reason for stepping down, but the board credited Tavares with leading the company's growth and strengthening its position in the credit scoring industry. "We thank Silvio Tavares for his five years of strong leadership of VantageScore," the board said in a statement. "During his tenure, VantageScore more than tripled its market presence and achieved numerous breakthroughs including widespread adoption in the U.S. mortgage credit-scoring market." Tavares said he was proud of the company's growth and its efforts to expand access to credit . "Together, we consistently delivered industry leading innovation and growth at a very high scale," Tavares said. "Along the way VantageScore responsibly expanded access to credit so that millions more creditworthy Americans can achieve their American dream." Hutchinson brings more than 30 years of experience in housing finance, public policy and industry leadership. Before joining VantageScore four years ago, he held senior positions at Freddie Mac , Fannie Mae and the National Association of Realtors . As interim CEO, Hutchinson said he plans to build on the company's momentum and continue expanding adoption of its credit scoring models. VantageScore 4.0 in particular has gained traction across the mortgage industry since the Federal Housing Finance Agency approved its use by lenders originating loans through Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. In September, FHFA Director Bill Pulte also announced that the government-sponsored enterprises would use a single loan-level price adjustment (LLPA) matrix regardless of which approved credit scoring model lenders use. "VantageScore is helping lenders make more predictive, inclusive and informed decisions across the credit lifecycle," Hutchinson said. "We are delivering strong business momentum and growing market adoption of the most predictive, innovative and inclusive tri-bureau models and attributes in the U.S. market." Related More: Credit Score Team Leaders VantageScore

items.title: Gencom-Led Partnership Acquires InterContinental Hotel In Downtown Miami
items.description: The 43-year-old InterContinental Miami has traded hands for the first time in more than 20 years. Courtesy of Gencom The more than 40-year-old hotel at 100 Chopin Plaza Miami-based companies Gencom and White Bridge Capital acquired the 652-key waterfront hotel from an entity tracing to Strategic Hotels & Resorts, which is owned by China's Daija Insurance Group, according to a release. Gencom declined to disclose the price. A person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg the sale totaled roughly $300M. “InterContinental Miami is a significant addition to Gencom’s portfolio and represents an important opportunity to deepen our presence in one of the most dynamic and globally recognized markets in the country,” Gencom Chief Investment Officer Alessandro Colantonio said in a statement. Strategic Hotels & Resorts purchased the hotel at 100 Chopin Plaza, next to Bayfront Park and right on the water, in 2005 for $52.2M, according to public records, though hotels often trade for more than their real estate values. Prior to the sale, Strategic Hotels & Resorts renovated the 34-story hotel's room interiors and the Club InterContinental Lounge and revamped the pool cabanas and SkyLawn outdoor event space. Gencom, a hospitality firm led by Karim Alibhai, and White Bridge Capital, which advises wealthy families primarily from Latin America and Southern Europe, plan to update the lobby and food and beverage options. “Given the recently completed renovation, we can focus on strengthening revenue across rooms, meetings and events, and dining while building on the enhanced guest experience in a market with substantial barriers to entry, the latter of which continues to be a key theme in the firm’s broader investment strategy,” Gencom Managing Director of Acquisitions Ignasi Puig said in a statement. The deal adds to the more than $1B Gencom has spent on acquiring luxury hotels on the East Coast over the last few years, primarily made up of Ritz-Carlton hotels, and most of which it is investing millions in for upgrades. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Hotel Investment Group by Northstar's Jeff Higley and Gencom's Karim Alibhai The firm acquired full control of the Marriott brand's Key Biscayne location for more than $400M in 2024 and bought back the majority stake in the Ritz-Carlton Coconut Grove at the beginning of the year. The firm also spent $320M in February on the 253-key Ritz-Carlton New York. Gencom also purchased another InterContinental-branded hotel in a joint venture for $230M in New York in December and spent $300M on the 587-room Thompson Central Park at the end of 2024. The company's acquisition strategy is largely driven toward assets where owners have been unable to reinvest in their properties , Alibhai said onstage at the Advisory, Lodging and Investment Summit for the Caribbean and Latin America in April. Alibhai told Bisnow in an interview in between panels at the conference that Gencom was searching for more acquisition targets in California, where multiple assets were involved in distressed sales . “You can have these situations that are distressed because they're just not positioned right,” Alibhai said onstage at the ALIS conference in April. “They're not managed to its fullest potential. They're starved for [capital expenditures].” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Gencom , InterContinental Miami , Karim Alibhai , Strategic Hotels & Resorts Inc

items.title: UK Budget Risks Deterring Sovereign Wealth Funds From Real Estate
items.description: The budget is out, and the property industry has concerns. UK Chancellor John Healey avoided a bond-market shock with his “breathing space” budget , and the immediate financial-market reaction was reassuring. Gilt yields did not spike, avoiding an outcome that could have pushed financing costs up even further. However, investors were left waiting for measures capable of bringing borrowing costs down and stimulating new development. The budget also delivered limited progress on development viability, while business rates measures offered some relief to high street occupiers without delivering the structural reform sought by many property owners. But new proposed tax rules for sovereign investors, which threaten to make the UK less attractive to global property capital, caused a sharp intake of breath. Flickr/House of Commons Chancellor John Healey succeeded in placating bond markets, but the property sector raised concerns over sovereign taxes. The government has launched a consultation over its proposal to replace the largely noncodified sovereign immunity from direct taxation with a statutory regime from 1 January 2029. Certain UK property income and capital gains would become taxable, although the reforms include bespoke access to the real estate investment trust regime, with a 15% tax rate on qualifying property income distributions. State-operated overseas pension funds and certain investment management activities would remain exempt. The government claimed the reforms would improve transparency and provide greater certainty for sovereign investors, but many in the property industry worry it could weaken the UK's appeal to investors. “It’s a really unhelpful change,” Real Estate:UK Assistant Director of Finance Rachel Kelly said. She said the proposal introduces additional costs for a significant source of real estate investment while development viability is already under severe pressure. Sovereign wealth funds invested £6.2B in UK property from 2021 to 2024, according to a March report from BPF and CoStar . Although the proposed REIT arrangements and transitional provisions offer some flexibility, the new 15% rate would be a significant increase for qualifying sovereign investors accustomed to paying no tax. It also adds an onerous process. “In addition to the actual additional cost now of investing in the UK for those investors, there will be huge complexity in terms of having to restructure their investments, and there will be a lot of work for some to change how they're structured,” Kelly said. The implications extend beyond the funds themselves. Sovereign wealth funds frequently invest alongside other capital providers, meaning changes to their investment structures could affect co-investors and joint ventures too, Moorfield CEO Charles Ferguson-Davie said. He said the reforms risk sending the wrong signal. “There aren’t that many groups that will deploy over £500M, over a billion,” Ferguson-Davie said. “If they’re going to be less active as a result of having to pay tax, who’s going to step in and invest that money instead?” CBRE Investment Management is looking to understand the rules in more detail during the consultation, Director Alex Lund said. But he expressed optimism that the policy won’t decimate investment. “For any market looking to attract overseas capital ... taxes and the need for a level playing field for domestic and international investors are very important,” he said. “But many investors are already in the UK, which is a large, deep and transparent market, so we would remain positive while looking at the consultation carefully.” Ferguson-Davie said the wider economic benefits of attracting large-scale investment should be part of the government's calculations, rather than focusing solely on the tax revenue generated. He said the string of regulatory or tax burdens added to the private rental sector over the last few budgets show the danger in the government’s thinking. “You can understand the political motivation, but it has already led to a lot of sales and exits from the market,” Ferguson-Davie said. “I'm not sure it's all necessarily ending up benefiting the renter.” Instead, supply and development have both fallen, and that pushes rents up. He said the new budget will encourage the sale of buy-to-lets, which could benefit the institutional build-to-rent sector — but it doesn’t actually solve any problems. “What the BTR community needs, indeed the housing sector needs, is more incentives to help bring down the cost of development,” he said. “If we're going to have a meaningful change in terms of new houses delivered for sale and for rent, we need the regulatory and tax burden reduced, because otherwise it's just going to get worse.” BTR construction starts have fallen 63% in the last year, with only 4,696 groundbreakings in September, versus 12,674 the year prior, according to Savills data for RE:UK . “Investors needed more than a pause in policy changes,” Kelly said. The budget's business rates package provided more immediate support for retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. However, Kelly said the chancellor again failed to deliver meaningful long-term reform. While the absence of another proposed surcharge on higher-value commercial property was welcome, RE:UK has called for the existing surcharge to be repealed and the tax system changed to make investment and refurbishment more attractive. Unsplash/Daniel Bond markets remained stable after the "breathing space" budget. The budget’s impact on London will be mixed, Knight Frank partner and Head of London Research Shabab Qadar said in a statement. The temporary increase in the bank surcharge could dampen a tenant pool that drives London’s global competitiveness, he said. And the policies do nothing to make more development more viable. “We would have liked to see more to unlock private capital, support the delivery of new commercial space and give London greater certainty over the infrastructure ne

items.title: Orchard Partners Selects JLL To Market 892K SF Manufacturing Campus In Brisbane: The San Francisco Deal Sheet
items.description: Lafayette-based real estate investment and development firm Orchard Partners selected JLL to market Quarry Innovation Center, a planned 892K SF advanced manufacturing campus in Brisbane. The campus will be on 61.4 acres at 1 Quarry Road, the site of a former rock quarry that opened in 1895 and supplied rock and aggregates to construction projects throughout the Bay Area. Wikimedia Commons/Derrick Coetzee The Guadalupe Quarry The project has been scaled back 33% from an original proposal to one two-story industrial building on previously disturbed quarry land, while the remaining 82 acres would be dedicated to permanent open space. An on-site substation would deliver 49 megawatts of power to the building for power-intensive advanced manufacturing tenants. A modern Class-A industrial building would be somewhat of a rarity on the San Francisco Peninsula — 77% of Mid-Peninsula industrial inventory was built prior to 1980, according to JLL researchers. “Our goal has been to thoughtfully balance land conservation and environmental stewardship of the quarry with the growing needs of modern industrial users,” Orchard Partners Managing Partner Tyler Higgins said in a statement. DevCon is the general contractor for the Quarry Innovation Center, with Ware Malcomb serving as project architect. Leasing will be handled by JLL’s Jason Ovadia, Greg Matter, Jason Cranston and Patrick Murdock. SALES Interstate Equities Corp. acquired the 2022-built The Dylan apartments at 2200 John Muir Parkway in Hercules for $83.5M from Hercules Development Partners. The property includes 217 market-rate keys and 15 below-market doors. JLL’s Capital Markets debt advisory team of Charles Halladay and Matt Cimino arranged a five-year acquisition loan through Freddie Mac for the buyer, while its investment and advisory sales team of Ryan Wagner, Brandon Geraldo, Matt Kroger and Fatai Alashe represented Hercules Development Partners. *** Carmel Partners of San Francisco acquired the 268-unit Silver apartment complex at 333 Sunol St. in central San Jose for $122M from an affiliate of Essex Property Trust. It is the fourth Bay Area transaction for Carmel Partners’ Carmel Fund 9. Built in 2018, Silver consists of studio, one- and two-bedroom units. Carmel plans to reposition the property through strategic upgrades to boost net operating income, Mike Ruiz, partner and head of acquisitions, said in a statement. *** Sausalito-based FH One Investments acquired a 1988-built, 106K SF office building at 500 Ygnacio Valley Road in Walnut Creek for $22.5M in a deed-in-lieu-of-foreclosure transaction. The building was about 70% leased and was purchased for a nearly 40% discount from what former owner Broadshore Capital Partners paid about a decade earlier. *** An affiliate of Oberndorf Real Estate Management and The Bascom Group purchased the 117-door Museum Park Apartments at 465 W. San Carlos St. in San Jose for $53.1M. An affiliate of Lakevision Capital purchased the 2002-built, Class-B garden-style multifamily property in 2020 for $57M. *** KKR and TMG partners acquired the 419K SF Skyport Plaza office and retail property in north San Jose from Hudson Pacific for $75.5M. Skyport Plaza consists of two mostly vacant eight-story office buildings and two occupied retail buildings. HPP said in a statement it will use sale proceeds to pay down an unsecured revolving credit facility, leaving a $30M balance. *** Marcus & Millichap’s Teodar Vacev of the firm’s Palo Alto office brokered the $5M sale of a 17K SF Caliber Collision repair facility at 3207 Shattuck Ave. in Berkeley to a private Bay Area-based investor. Marcus & Millichap’s Kirk Trammell and Josh Johnson represented the buyer in purchase negotiations. *** TruAmerica Multifamily of Los Angeles acquired Bridges at San Ramon, a 1988-built garden-style multifamily community of 200 doors, for $78M from Acacia Capital. The property, located near the 585-acre Bishop Ranch mixed-use office hub, hadn’t changed hands in the past 15 years and saw strong investor interest. Jason Parr, Scott MacDonald, Sydney Ladrech and John Hansen of Berkadia’s San Francisco office arranged the sale on behalf of San Mateo-based Acacia Capital. *** The Davis Cos. of Boston acquired a 65K SF office and research and development building at 51 Rio Robles in San Jose for $17M. Maxeon Solar Technologies is the sole tenant at the facility, which features 3,000 amps of power. The Davis Cos. plans to reposition the property in 2027 with a new roof, upgraded mechanical and HVAC systems, and interior improvements. Colliers’ Andy Zighelboim, Kevin Moul, Brad Idleman and Bob Gilley brokered the purchase on behalf of The Davis Cos. *** Sterling Organization of West Palm Beach, Florida, acquired two Bay Area grocery-anchored retail centers through its Sterling United Properties fund. Safeway Burlingame is a 70K SF, 100% leased retail center on the Peninsula, while Pleasanton Gateway Shopping Center is a 128K SF, 99% leased center in the East Bay that is also anchored by Safeway. CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Santa Clara County completed the new 77-bed Behavioral Health Pavilion at Santa Clara Valley Medical Center. The three-story, 207K SF building at 751 S. Bascom Ave. in San Jose was designed by HGA and built by Webcor. *** DM Development of San Francisco and Denver-based private equity firm Ascentris secured $61.7M in construction financing from PNC Bank to build a 152-key, nine-story multifamily property at 321 Florida St. in San Francisco’s Mission District. Handel Architects of San Francisco is designing the building, which will include 15 affordable units. Groundbreaking is expected to commence in November, with completion slated for late 2028. *** Standard Communities broke ground on two affordable housing communities totaling 428 new doors in Antioch. The $192M Joyfield Flats at Lakeview Center and Joyfield Flats at Buchanan Crossing are expected to be developed for less than $500K

items.title: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Could Expand In North Texas
items.description: Another semiconductor industry power player is reportedly eyeing North Texas' Silicon Prairie for its next chip fabrication plant. Wikimedia Commons/Peellden Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s Fab 5 building in Taiwan Sherman has been identified as the leading candidate to score Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co .’s next massive fabrication facility, which could bring an investment of $120B, the Dallas Business Journal reported . State documents the DBJ obtained say TSMC locating its next facility in Sherman would make the most sense. Those documents indicated an unnamed semiconductor manufacturer is seeking sites in Texas for a $45B investment in the construction of two plants. However, Bloomberg reported earlier this month that TSMC was considering the Dallas-Fort Worth area for as many as six semiconductor facilities that would each carry a $20B price tag. TSMC⁠ CEO C.C. Wei said during an Oct. 15 earnings call that the company’s U.S. customers have requested it expand beyond its existing fabrication facility in Phoenix. “We are moving full speed ahead to increase our capacity to meet our assessed demand and stepping up our capex investment to support our customers' future growth,” Wei said. “TSMC is expanding at an unprecedented pace with nearly 20 fabs worldwide in progress.” Central Texas is also being considered for TSMC's semiconductor expansion, the Austin Business Journal reported . Sherman, a city around 60 miles north of Dallas, has become the centerpiece of North Texas' Silicon Prairie push. It has lined up more than $40B in investments in massive semiconductor plants from Texas Instruments , GlobalWafers and Coherent. The city’s abundant land and prodigious water supply have been key to its success in attracting semiconductor plants, which is why the Grayson County municipality is seen as the leading candidate for TSMC's expansion. “I think the water that they have [in Sherman] is the only location in our market that I'm aware of that has the volume in capacity to feed that type of engine,” North Texas land broker Rex Glendenning told the DBJ. Sherman officials said the city hasn’t been contacted about TSMC's planned expansion. Fort Worth has also had success in attracting more companies connected to the semiconductor industry in recent years. items.title: CCM's VantageScore test saves $2,500; rivals lock FICO deals
items.description: CCM's VantageScore test saves $2,500; rivals lock FICO deals By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 30, 2026, 4:52 p.m. EDT | Updated October 30, 2026, 5:36 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Find out why some major mortgage lenders are signing on for FICO's bundled pricing and how much another prominent player says VantageScore has been saving them on certain loans. Expert Quote: "A 740 classic FICO isn't necessarily the same risk as a 740 VantageScore loan." — Sandra Thompson, former director, Federal Housing Finance Agency Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Some lenders have signed up for FICO's bundle while another one has found savings in government-sponsored enterprises' unified loan pricing for VantageScore 4.0, highlighting new drivers for how the industry is making choices around credit metrics. Fairway, Movement and Rate reported Friday that they have committed to FICO's bundle , which pledges a price freeze for commitments, while CrossCountry Mortgage found that a 60-day test of VantageScore 4.0 generated an average of $2,500 in savings on some loans. Processing Content "This demonstrates how additional flexibility can translate into meaningful benefits for our customers," Brian Clark, director of product and pricing at CCM, said in a press release, while noting that it's part of broader moves to fully use government-related market options to this end. Brian Clark, CrossCountry Mortgage CCM also is removing a 80% loan-to-value ratio cap it has had as an overlay for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans, allowing some borrowers to exceed this, and also giving borrowers broader access to Department of Veterans Affairs-guaranteed loans. Meanwhile, Rocket Mortgage also has found VS4 offers some advantages in a five-month test of 1.4 million customers, CEO Jay Bray said at Housing Finance Strategies' conference this week. Rocket reported earlier that it would be making VantageScore its default credit metric . "We saw higher approval. We saw customers being able to save money, and so we made the choice to move in that direction for certain pieces of our portfolio," he told listeners to the conference, which HFS broadcast online. Lenders sees a need for both score providers for now VS4 has become more competitive in the GSEs' market since their oversight agency unified the pricing for loans based on it with FICO's longtime industry standard, removing a previous adjustment, but so far lenders are still reporting a need for both credit metrics. "Since VantageScore 4.0 isn't accepted across all programs yet, this approach gives loan officers more flexibility," CCM said in its emailed statement. Executives from Fairway, Rate and Movement all also issued statements that show a persistent need for FICO scores in a press release. "We will continue to evaluate FICO Scores in our wide range of eligible loan products and programs," Stacey Sprain, senior vice president of credit and vendor support at Fairway Home Mortgage, said in one such statement. VantageScore 4.0 and a newer FICO 10T score slated for later enterprise adoption both differ from the latter's traditional credit metric for mortgages in that they both incorporate more data such as borrower payments over time as opposed to a snapshot of the borrower's obligations. While CrossCountry has reported some early savings related to current GSE loan pricing with no differentiation for FICO classic and VS4 scores, former Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Sandra Thompson said this week she had some concerns about it. Ex-officials' take on current loan pricing for scores "The most important aspect of credit modernization is getting the risk pricing of the loans done correctly," Thompson said. "A 740 classic FICO isn't necessarily the same risk as a 740 VantageScore loan," she said during the Housing Finance Strategies conference. Scores the GSEs use in loan pricing have broad impacts for them and their counterparties that Thompson said should be given more consideration before treating them in a unified manner. Sandra Thompson "Capital is absolutely going to be impacted. The mortgage insurers are looking at these numbers as well," Thompson said. Both she and her fellow HFS conference panelist Alanna McCargo, who previously served as president of Ginnie Mae and then later of the Federal Home Loan Bank of San Francisco, called for more data around such implications. "I just think we need to be very careful as this rolls out," McCargo said. items.title: Lenders race to arm LOs with AI to boost capacity
items.description: Lenders race to arm LOs with AI to boost capacity By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 30, 2026, 3:18 p.m. EDT | Updated October 30, 2026, 3:57 p.m. EDT 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Loan officers ability to handle heavier workloads without sacrificing responsiveness to borrowers. Expert Quote: "Technology can help identify what fits within published guidelines, but it cannot replace the value of experience" — Marc Halpern, CEO, Foundation Mortgage Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content Mortgage lenders and their technology providers are racing to put artificial intelligence in loan officers' hands, betting it will let originators handle more loans without slowing response times to borrowers. In recent weeks, non-QM wholesaler Foundation Mortgage launched AskClara, an AI assistant that answers brokers' plain-language questions about products and eligibility. Dark Matter Technologies bought House Numbers' AI agent platform, and nCino rolled out an AI-driven productivity suite for loan officers. What Foundation Mortgage's AskClara does Non-qualified mortgage wholesaler Foundation Mortgage has created an artificial intelligence assistant for its mortgage brokers to get product information and more. The company has named this piece of technology AskClara, and it will give advice in response to plain language questions asked by mortgage broker users. Besides products, AskClara will also return any underwriting criteria, documentation options and potential eligibility. "One of the biggest challenges brokers face with non-QM lending is understanding the full range of options available for borrowers who don't fit conventional guidelines," said Marc Halpern, CEO of Foundation, in a press release. "Our goal is to help brokers recognize opportunities earlier, ask better questions, and find solutions for more borrowers." Marc Halpern is the CEO of Foundation Mortgage The company pointed out AskClara is a tool to identify potential borrower eligibility based on published program guidelines across various types of non-QM products like debt service coverage ratio , bank statement, asset qualifier, closed end seconds and others, but it will not perform automated underwriting or make credit approvals. "Technology can help identify what fits within published guidelines, but it cannot replace the value of experience, judgment, and the willingness to take a closer look," Halpern said. Importantly, even if AskClara gives a negative response, it is not Foundation giving the broker a no. "We want brokers to use the technology to start the conversation, not end it," Halpern said. "That's what common-sense underwriting is all about." A pair of offerings out of nCino For third-party originators who use the ICE Mortgage Technology Encompass LOS, nCino has created TPO Experience for its point of sale system. It will allow Encompass retail originators to use the same platform for their wholesale production, nCino said. Lenders can have brokers submit loans through the same technology their in-house loan officers use. Brokered loans are assigned to a loan officer at the wholesaler. They are then synced to Encompass with the appropriate channel designation and third-party originators information. It allows the lender's existing business rules to apply for brokered loans. "Growth in the wholesale channel is putting more pressure on lenders to eliminate the operational divide between their retail and wholesale businesses," said Casey Williams, general manager of global mortgage at nCino in the press release. "TPO Experience gives lending teams a consistent, efficient path to originate loans, no matter how they come in." The September announcement added nCino plans to expand support to additional LOS systems. Separately, in October, nCino introduced the Loan Officer Productivity Suite, which it called a comprehensive set of AI-driven tools for mortgage salespersons. It uses the lender's own data, product guidelines and workflow rules to give originators institution-specific answers. The suite consists of the following modules: Mortgage Advisor for Loan Officers Loan PreCheck Mortgage MCP for Loan Officers AUS Smart Tasks Automated Pre-approval Automated Disclosures "Loan officers are being asked to handle more work without sacrificing responsiveness to borrowers," Williams said in this press release. "The Loan Officer Productivity Suite helps create that capacity by taking routine work off originators' plates and putting answers and next steps at their fingertips, so they can stay responsive and competitive without adding more hours to the day." Dark Matter acquires House Numbers' AI technology Dark Matter Technologies has purchased House Numbers' platform which creates artificial intelligence agents for home lending workflows. The deal also includes the related intellectual property. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. In addition, the team responsible for this technology is joining Dark Matter as part of the deal. It includes House Numbers co-founder and CEO Jeff Levinsohn, who joins Dark Matter as chief AI officer. Dark Matter had been the origination technology business of Black Knight ; it was divested as part of the ICE Mortgage Technology deal. As part of the divestiture, Dark Matter ended up with Aiva. So it already has AI working inside its loan process and this made his team interested in joining forces, Levinsohn said in the press release. This latest Dark Matter purchase accelerates agentic AI across the Empower loan origination solution and its built-in point of sale technology. The company said it will allow lenders to use autonomous AI agents and AI agent assistants to improve borrower experiences, increase loan officer productivity, lower the cost of origination and advance the shift from doing to reviewing. items.title: DSCR fraud suits: Flag repeat appraisers and title agents
items.description: DSCR fraud suits: Flag repeat appraisers and title agents By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published October 30, 2026, 1:28 p.m. EDT 6 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Uncover how fraudsters used mismatched appraisal photos to secure inflated real estate loans. What's at Stake: Legitimate real estate development and municipal revitalization efforts are jeopardized by widespread foreclosure schemes. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content A new lawsuit in a Baltimore fraud scandal is shining the spotlight on risks posed in real estate investment lending as well as the civic harm caused when scams become widespread. The broadening scandal involves dozens of homes purchased by alleged ringleaders of the scheme: Eluzer Gold, Benjamin Eidlisz and Shraga Lerner. The three are accused of acquiring properties, many of which were vacant, rundown or in otherwise poor condition and securing inflated appraisals after supposed renovations, before selling the units to entities run by Gold, who secured the homes with debt-service-coverage-ratio loans from Commercial Lender and RCN Capital. The details of the case demonstrate the importance of fraud recognition and vigilance when it comes to dealing with vendors throughout the purchase process, particularly in investor real estate . The two mortgage lenders, listed as plaintiffs in the civil case, originated 59 loans to the group, and saw financial losses of more than $10 million when liens went delinquent and homes were foreclosed upon. The plaintiffs accuse Gold, Eidlisz and Lerner of fraud, conspiracy in violating the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act among other charges. "The fraudsters shared a common purpose of purchasing distressed properties and reselling them to the borrowers at prices that materially exceeded the properties' true market value," the lawsuit said. "Each fraudster knowingly agreed that at least one member of the conspiracy would commit racketeering acts," it continued. Also listed as defendants in the late-September legal filing are dozens of businesses and individuals in the appraisal and title industry, including Christopher Actie and Jason Taylor. The two Maryland-based appraisers provided valuations for all but one of the units in question on behalf of a variety of management companies, also named as defendants. Clear Capital, along with several of its employees or agents who were assigned to perform independent desk reviews of the appraisals and approved them prior to loan disbursement, was also served papers. Charges against the individuals and appraisal firms included unjust enrichment, professional malpractice and negligent misrepresentation. The case comes on the heels of a similar lawsuit filed a few weeks earlier by wholesale lender AmeriTrust Mortgage Corp. against the same primary parties as well as broker FirstLoans, who facilitated the originations. That lawsuit involves 90 properties, with losses from the fraud costing AmeriTrust an estimated $14 million. The developments were first reported by the Baltimore Banner. Attorneys for the leading defendants were not listed, while Clear Capital said it could not comment on pending litigation. Lawyers claim the total number of homes purchased and foreclosed upon in the defendants' scheme could approach 500. The timeline of events In the scheme that ran between mid 2023 and early 2024, companies belonging to Lerner purchased the Baltimore properties, sometimes with financial assistance from Eidlisz. Arrangements were subsequently made to sell the homes to Gold, who applied for the fraudulent loans from Commercial and RCN with Eidlisz facilitating the process. While original purchase prices ranged between $40,000 and $100,000, resale values came in two to five times higher following the appraisals of supposedly renovated properties. Most of the homes purchased, however, were flipped and sold within weeks, an unreasonably short time frame for homes to undergo full renovation. The lawsuit also noted that photographs used in the appraisals did not match the home involved. Attorneys for the plaintiffs pointed to mismatches in the appraisal reports with listing photographs, such as inconsistencies in layouts and floor plans. "Appraisers used photographs that were not photographs of the subject property but instead depicted a superior property and used those false photographs, in part, to support an inflated valuation," the legal document said. Based on the purported value of the homes, plaintiffs applied loan-to-value ratios to originate mortgages that were $80,000 to over $130,000 more than the price of the original purchases, with the perpetrators pocketing the proceeds, before allowing the properties to go into foreclosure. Two firms named as defendants managed the vast majority of the resale closings: Commerce Title and Rextar Title. The two had also participated in the initial purchases of the same units by Gold and thus should have been aware of the rapid turnaround time and value of the properties, attorneys said. Despite having inside institutional knowledge about the Baltimore market, the firms were negligent and failed in their fiduciary duties in neglecting to disclose unusual activity and agreeing to close the resale, according to legal counsel. Upon discovery of fraud in the first half of 2024, the lenders immediately ceased working with Gold. The three alleged perpetrators then targeted AmeriTrust to prolong their scheme, submitting their first application to the company in April that year. Commercial Lender and RCN Capital are seeking monetary damages of more than $12.2 million, which includes accrued interest and profits made from the illegal resales. items.description: A tree-lined retreat nestled beneath a “canopy of magnificent mature oaks,” featuring illuminated pathways, has recently hit the market in Topanga, CA , for $2.4 million. Built in 1935, the “thoughtfully cared for” 1,547-square-foot sanctuary boasts stone pathways, footbridges, and a seasonal creek. It is located in the Post Office Tract near Topanga State Park. “What makes this property so special is its setting within a private oak grove,” says listing agent Nina Kurtz of Compass . “It genuinely feels like having your own private park.” That private-park feel extends across the compound, which includes a two-bedroom primary residence and additional living space. Loading... The compound in Topanga, CA, features garden-lined paths. Anthony Barcelo Loading... The sun-soaked kitchen has direct access to the outdoor living area. Anthony Barcelo Loading... items.title: In Midterm Toss-Up States of Ohio, Iowa, Texas, and Maine, Housing Affordability Is Top of Mind
items.description: As the country heads into the final days before the 2026 midterm elections, housing affordability weighs heavily on many voters’ minds. A recent Pew Research Center poll found that 66% of Americans are “very concerned” about housing costs. And this past July, CNBC’s All-America Economic Survey found that housing affordability is the top concern for Gen Z voters and men aged 18 to 44. That’s likely because Americans are spending more money—and more of their incomes—on housing than they have in recent memory. A 2024 study from Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that nearly half of all Americans—49%—spend more than the recommended 30% of their income on housing. Yet lawmakers and voters remain divided on how to ease the economic burden so many Americans now face. Is it an issue of building more housing or backing more programs to subsidize rents and mortgages? Will raising wages solve the problem, or will creating more tenant protections offer relief? Or is the answer some combination of all of the above? That's why, ahead of the 2026 midterms, Realtor.com® examined the housing issues animating voters in the four states that Decision Desk HQ has deemed Senate race toss-ups, with no clear leader in the polls: Maine , Iowa , Ohio , and Texas . The goal was to understand better how housing issues are animating voters and what residents hope lawmakers will do once elected. Despite radically different local environments, several common themes emerged: People feel that owning a home has become increasingly out of reach. They worry about people on the lowest end of the economic spectrum. They are also skeptical that an election will really change much. Read on to learn what housing advocates and average citizens across Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Maine want lawmakers to focus on after the electionn. Maine voters are a mix of newcomers and longtime landowners In the race for Maine's Senate seat, Democrat Troy Jackson is narrowly favored to defeat longtime incumbent Susan Collins , a Republican. Both agree that private equity investment in residential properties was a major problem in the state, though they don’t necessarily agree on how to solve it. Jackson criticized Collins for voting against an amendment from Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH) that would support building 7 million new homes and expanding affordable housing opportunities. Collins has criticized Jackson for claiming two homes as primary residences for tax benefits. Dan Martin, 41, and his family moved to Freeport, ME , from New Jersey five years ago, trading proximity to New York City for more space and a better quality of life. He’s one of more than 126,000 people who have moved to Maine since 2020, and he says he was struck by the disparity in housing access in the state. “Landowners here own a lot of land, and they’re often unwilling to give it up,” he says. “And that’s fine, but it does create a disparity in what’s available. “We have a wide breadth of wealthy generational Mainers alongside Somalian refugees," he continues. "And we don’t have enough housing—low-income housing for those folks." The National Low Income Housing Coalition estimates that Maine has a shortage of 20,000 rental homes for extremely low-income residents. Wages in the state also haven’t kept up with housing costs. At the state minimum wage of $15.10 an hour, a worker must put in 67 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment at a fair market price of $1,323 a month, according to NLIHC . Loading... The town hall in Bangor, ME, is equipped with voting booths for early midterm voting on Oct. 16, 2026. Americans voting in the Nov. 3 elections will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency. AFP via Getty Images Ohioans want affordable and 'attainable' housing On Tuesday, Republican incumbent John Husted faces Democrat challenger Sherrod Brown in the Ohio race for U.S. Senate. Brown, a former Senator, narrowly leads in the polls, according to Decision Desk . Hu s ted ’s campaign has stressed increasing the housing supply, cutting federal regulations, and enabling private investment rather than direct government funding. Brown favors lowering housing costs, expanding inventory, and protecting affordable housing. Sonya Fix is a professor at Columbus College of Art and Design in Columbus, OH , and has lived in the city on and off for most of her life. She purchased her home in 2018, but says that many of her fellow 40-something friends are struggling to do so now. "I’ve seen friends who are even in better positions than me not be able to buy a house. All of a sudden, during the [COVID-19] pandemic, everyone wanted to buy a house, and rates started going up. So I consider myself pretty lucky to have bought what I did." Some of those friends "might have owned a house at one point but got divorced and have been renting. You know, it's just, it's really hard to reenter the market as a buyer now because houses are so expensive." Some of her friends who are renting are also feeling the squeeze. "I am just absolutely shocked. I have no clue how working-class, lower-income, or even lower-middle-class families who have to rent are doing it," she says. Apartments that once rented for $500 to $600 a month now cost twice as much. Fix would like to see stronger tenant protections, especially since two-bedroom rents in Ohio increased 28% between January 2020 and January 2025, according to the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio . "Especially in Columbus and the surrounding areas, where there's a lot of big tech coming in,” she says. "There has to be rental protections to allow people to stay in their homes as opposed to getting shoved out so that the landlord can get someone with more money." Marcus Roth , communications director of the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio, sees the housing crisis in the state as a multipronged problem, one that’s no longer just an issue for low-income Americans.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: ‘Members Only: Palm Beach’ Star Hilary Musser Reveals Plans for New Show With a Possible Real Estate Twist
items.description: “Members Only: Palm Beach” star Hilary Musser is working on a new TV project that could incorporate the area’s luxury real estate —and says she would also serve as a producer. While the future of the Netflix hit remains uncertain, Musser says she is already pursuing another opportunity, with casting among the steps she is working on. “I’m working on a different show right now,” she says. It's a project “where I would also be a producer.” Musser is keeping most of the details private for now. She says the network has not been determined, but the Palm Beach County setting could provide an opening to feature the industry in which she has built her business. “In Palm Beach County, we’re famous for our real estate,” she says. Loading... “Members Only: Palm Beach” star Hilary Musser is working on a new TV project that could incorporate the area’s luxury real estate—and says she would also serve as a producer. Hilary Musser However, she does not envision creating a series focused entirely on property. Instead, she says real estate could be one element of a broader concept. The project comes as Musser considers what she wants to do following her appearance on “Members Only: Palm Beach.” The series has not been canceled nor renewed. “It doesn’t really matter to me if the show gets renewed,” she says. Her introduction to that series came through fellow cast member Taja Abitbol , whom she met while serving on a fundraising committee. During a cocktail party, Abitbol asked whether she would be interested in interviewing for a TV show about country club life in Palm Beach. Musser agreed, having previously passed on other opportunities to appear on camera. She says she was approached about a Palm Beach housewives show in 2005, but declined after being filmed because she worried about the potential impact on her marriage and young son. This time, she decided to embrace the opportunity. During filming, Musser says she did not prepare dialogue or attempt to adopt a different personality. With a real estate business to consider, she wanted to present herself as she normally would. “I didn’t prepare what I was going to say,” she says. Alongside her TV appearance, Musser was also working on a waterfront spec home that she says was completed in June and is now offered for $42.5 million. The property is a development she built to sell. Separately, she describes her personal home as smaller but similarly finished. According to Musser, the spec home sits along the Intracoastal Waterway, across from the Palm Beach property being developed by billionaire Ken Griffin . Inside, she says the emphasis is on distinctive finishes and an uncompromising approach to quality, with leather-wrapped refrigerator handles, leather-lined kitchen drawers, Italian marble, and a separate chef’s kitchen. “Every door is 12 feet high,” she says. For Musser, those details reflect what she believes wealthy buyers want: a property that offers something different from other luxury homes, with spaces that provide their own reasons to stay in. Rather than approaching a development solely as something to sell, she considers whether she would enjoy living there herself. “And I build every house as if I’m going to live in it,” she says. Musser initially obtained her real estate license to improve her access to properties for her development business. She felt desirable opportunities were being claimed before reaching the market and wanted to put herself in a better position to find them. After working with a friend for a couple of years, she earned her broker’s license. Representing clients was not originally the goal, but requests from people in her community led her to begin showing and listing homes. She says her real estate business’ gross revenue quadrupled last year, and she regards her TV experience as a success from a business perspective. items.title: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity?
items.description: Beyond the Rent: What is the true cost of your equity? Many owners face the challenge of bringing more money into their deal. Sometimes, the cost may outweigh the benefits. Published Oct. 30, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . These days, it feels like you can find a stat to support just about anything you want. Think inflation isn’t an issue? If you watch the Sunday political shows long enough, someone probably has numbers to support that notion. On the other side, there’s probably someone who can tell you that the third-quarter U.S. real gross domestic product growth of 3.4% is a mirage. Think Brian Schottenheimer isn’t getting enough out of the Dallas Cowboys? (Spoiler alert: he isn’t, despite this week's win.) The folks at Pro Football Focus probably have something to back those claims. The same is true in multifamily. Since I started covering this sector, the number of studies, surveys and indexes that fill my inbox each day seems to have quadrupled … at least. I delete most of these research projects or studies because much of this “research” is sent under the guise of pitching products. However, I do look at certain reports and even seek others out. As more loans face issues in the apartment industry, I recently went to CRED iQ’s website to get an idea of the size of the maturity wall. There I found something that caught my eye — an article saying nearly 33% of maturing apartment debt needs a cash infusion to refinance. At first blush, that number felt, well, kind of low, given everything that I’ve been reading about maturity walls and refinance risk. Reading further on the CRED iQ website, I learned that the firm resized every multifamily loan in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and commercial mortgage-backed securities deals maturing between October 2026 and December 2028. Of that $136 billion in debt, 23% of the loans and 31% of the balance can’t refinance without an equity infusion of roughly $6.8 billion. The good news for apartment owners is that money is available to fill that gap. The bad news: It’s getting more expensive. Earlier this year, Maximiliane Leachman, vice chair of CBRE’s debt and structured finance group, told me refinancing is becoming harder for some borrowers. At one point, these lenders may have wanted 1% to 3% of the loan balance for an extension. Now, many could be looking for 10%. “We’re all waiting for the shoe to drop at the end of this year as those borrowers come back for the second time to that debt fund for another modification,” Leachman said. “It will be interesting to see how many of those go back.” But costs aren’t the only issues owners must weigh when deciding whether to bring additional capital into their deals. In a recent conversation, Michael Lynd, CEO of Kairoi Residential, raised another concern: whether refinancing is worth the cost to existing equity holders. “The question that I have when I look at a lot of these refinances is the cost of that refinance is not great for your existing equity,” Lynd said. “If rent growth doesn’t show up in that first six to nine months or a year, then you have a chance of further impairing the equity value that isn't in place.” Lynd thinks a lot of groups are making decisions that might not be in their investors’ best interests by holding on to properties rather than selling them because they don’t want a negative trade on their record. Alternatively, they may want to delay a sale to raise additional capital. “I see it happening all over the place,” Lynd said. “You can get a loan, but should you take that loan? Is that the best risk-adjusted decision for your equity?” If the answer is no and if the market doesn’t snap back, those firms might be doing their investors a disservice. Still, some owners may find data showing refinancing is the best option. And it could be. But just because you can find the data to say something doesn’t make it so. items.title: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers – Insurance Business
items.description: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers A White House plan to pull private mortgage insurance off loans sooner, and to let refinancing borrowers skip the lender's title policy, affects two insurance lines that say they already help keep costs down PROPERTY By Stephen Owens Oct 25, 2026 Share Mortgage insurers and title underwriters are the latest targets of the White House's pre-election push on housing costs. President Donald Trump on Oct. 22 signed an executive order, Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People , that leans on the Federal Housing Finance Agency to squeeze costs out of the mortgage process. Two of its four main provisions deal with insurance: a pilot to cancel mortgage insurance premiums ahead of schedule, and a permanent version of FHFA's experiment letting some refinances skip the traditional lender's title policy, according to the White House fact sheet . The rest of the order sets up a federal task force on factory-built housing and tells the Agriculture and Veterans Affairs departments to cut rates on their direct home loans. FHFA Director Bill Pulte called it "the greatest Housing Executive Order in History" on X. The fact sheet, however, sets no equity thresholds, no start dates and no estimate of how many loans would qualify, so mortgage insurers, title underwriters and agents can't yet tell how much business is at stake. Read next: Why home insurance prices are quietly becoming a 2026 midterm flashpoint Mortgage insurers say cancellation rules already exist The mortgage insurance piece would have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac use automated valuation models to recheck home values on loans they own from time to time, then drop the coverage once a borrower appears to have built enough equity, according to Mortgage Professional America's breakdown of the order . Servicers would have to tell borrowers when cancellation might be possible. The pilot covers only loans originated after it launches. Borrowers already paying premiums would not benefit directly. Mortgage insurers point out that borrowers already have cancellation rights. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, borrower-paid coverage on a conventional loan must end automatically once the balance hits 78% of the home's original value, and borrowers can ask to cancel at 80%, with some able to qualify on the strength of home price gains if conditions are met, according to U.S. Mortgage Insurers (USMI) , the trade group whose members include Enact, Essent, MGIC, National MI and Radian. USMI President Seth Appleton welcomed the focus on costs and said the industry was already lowering them. "Private MI is designed to be temporary, and the system already works much the way the order envisions, because when MI is cancelled, a borrower's monthly payment goes down," he said in the group's statement. USMI's statement describes the order as telling FHFA to consider a pilot, not to launch one. The group says premium rates have fallen 25% since 2017, that more than 800,000 buyers used private coverage in 2025, two-thirds of them first-timers, and that its members insure more than $1.6 trillion in mortgages. Insurers have paid over $62 billion in claims since 2008 that would otherwise have hit the government-sponsored enterprises, lenders and investors, USMI said. The pilot could also affect pricing. Mortgage insurance is priced on how long an insurer expects to keep collecting premiums. Some industry voices warned that a program clipping off late-life, low-risk loans could push insurers to build that lost income into pricing on new business, MPA reported . The order comes during a strong year for mortgage insurers. New insurance written across the six active private insurers (Arch, Enact, Essent, MGIC, NMI and Radian) hit a multi-year high in the second quarter of 2026, with strong credit performance, according to Milliman's quarterly market update . Read next : Old Republic prevails as Massachusetts court rejects title coverage expansion Title waiver pilot would become permanent For title underwriters, the order expands a program their trade group has opposed since 2024. The title acceptance pilot dates to March 2024, when the Biden-era FHFA approved waiving the lender's title policy, or an attorney opinion letter, on certain low-risk refinances where there is confidence the property is free of prior liens, according to a statement from then-Director Sandra Thompson . Fannie Mae launched it in November 2024 with Doma Title Insurance and added Westcor Land Title Insurance Co. in July 2025. Pulte said in June that Fannie would grow it. The order would make the program permanent and broaden it. The order directs FHFA to lift the current 80% loan-to-value cap on eligibility, bring in more title-assessment providers and scrap the geographic limits, according to MPA's reading of the text. It also calls for waiving appraisals and income re-verification on limited cash-out refinances that cut a borrower's monthly payment. The American Land Title Association responded the same day, warning that any cost-cutting push must keep protections for homeowners and their property rights in place rather than shift risk to consumers and taxpayers. In 2024, ALTA called the original pilot a political gesture that offered a false promise of savings. Analysts expect a limited effect for now. Analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods wrote in an Oct. 21 note that refinances account for only about 7% of title premiums, so the earnings hit should be modest while the program stays refi-only. They said the risk would be greater if the waiver ever reached purchase loans, where there is no scalable substitute for a title policy. Refinance volume is low with 30-year rates above 7%, but a rate drop would quickly enlarge the pool of loans eligible for a waiver, and the order would also remove the program's geographic limits. items.title: Q3 2026 U.S. Multifamily Figures
items.description: Figures Multifamily Rents Rise Slightly as New Construction Slows U.S. Multifamily | Q3 2026 October 30, 2026 2 Minute Read Looking for a PDF of this content? Download Executive Summary The overall multifamily vacancy rate rose by 40 basis points (bps) in Q3 to 4.7%, as completions outpaced net absorption for the first time since Q4 2025. Net absorption totaled 8,747 units in Q3, down from 42,166 a year ago and bringing the year-to-date total to 260,500 units. Average monthly rent increased by 1% year-over-year in Q3 and 0.5% quarter-over-quarter to $2,268. Construction completions totaling 85,300 units fell by 11% year-ovrer-year in Q3. Multifamily investment volume rose by 140% year-over-year in Q3 to $112.3 billion due to a $69.6 billion entity-level transaction. Excluding that deal, volume was down by 8.7%. Individual asset sales declined by 15% to $32.7 billion, while portfolio sales increased by 20.7% to $10 billion.

Supply & Demand Throughout the year, a total of 4,135 units across 13 buildings were delivered, up 2.3% year-over-year (YOY). At the end of Q3, there were 22 buildings under construction totaling 6,806 units, with 54.8% of that activity located in Hillsborough County. Starts were down to 672 units from the 3,104 units recorded at the peak over the past five years. The decrease in new units being built should help rebalance supply and demand. This coupled with projected higher long-term interest rates and hindered homebuying could provide more time for newly completed developments to reach stabilized occupancy. Additionally, rising building material costs and upward pressure on labor expenses are also constraining new development activity, further limiting future supply and creating near-term breathing room for existing and newly completed assets. Total absorption through Q3 2026 reached over 1,700 units, up from the 160 units recorded one year ago. Stabilized occupancy (which excludes properties in initial lease-up or delivered within the past 18 months) fell to 91.6%. Several submarkets continued to post strong occupancy rates, including Downtown St. Petersburg (94.3%), Downtown Tampa (93.9%) and Northwest Tampa (93.8%). These submarkets are supported by favorable supply-demand dynamics, proximity to key employment centers, and comparatively limited competitive deliveries. Market Pricing Effective rents declined 1.6% YOY. This was attributed to increased availability in lower-tier, older developments as residents shift toward high-end options amid expanding new supply and more competitive concession offerings. Hillsborough County recorded the most substantial rental dip, down 2.3% YOY, followed by Pinellas County, down 0.4% during the same period. Despite recent rent declines, the limited pipeline of new construction in Tampa Bay is expected to tighten future supply conditions. As demand stabilizes, this constrained development outlook should support and ultimately elevate rental rates across the market. Investment Activity Tampa’s multifamily investment market remained strong through Q3, with the five-year total sales volume reaching $14.2 billion, the second-highest volume in Florida behind Orlando. items.description: Share: Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn I recommend visiting cushmanwakefield.com to read:%0A%0A {0} %0A%0A {1} Insights Tucson Industrial MarketBeat This MarketBeat report covers the Tucson industrial real estate market for Q3 2026, including narrative insights on the economy, supply and demand, and pricing. Read the report for the full details. DOWNLOAD THE Q3 2026 REPORT Key Takeaways Tucson's economy continued to expand modestly in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, though the signals were mixed. Unemployment rose to 5.0% from 4.3% a year ago, above both the U.S. (4.2%) and Phoenix (4.4%). In Q3 2026, Tucson's industrial vacancy declined slightly to 7.7%, with YTD net absorption reaching 379,171 sf reflecting continued leasing activity through the market. Average asking rents remained stable at $0.92 psf per month NNN, with market conditions generally balanced as newer industrial projects competed for tenants. A notable transaction during the quarter was the sale of a 14-property small bay industrial portfolio, sold by Equus Capital Partners to Everview Partners L.P . for $165.75 million. Economy Tucson's economy continued to expand modestly in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, though the signals were mixed. Unemployment rose to 5.0% from 4.3% a year ago, above both the U.S. (4.2%) and Phoenix (4.4%). This can be read as a softening labor market, or as an expanding labor force drawing more residents into the job search. Household fundamentals were stronger. Median household income rose 4.8% to $79,200, outpacing national growth of 3.9%, and household formation grew 0.9% to 457,000, nearly double the U.S. rate. Incomes still trail the national median of $88,400 by about 10%. Moody's Analytics expects unemployment to ease toward 4.5% by Q3 2027. The main headwind remains financing: the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.64% from 4.26% a year ago. Supply & Demand In Q3 2026, Tucson's industrial vacancy declined slightly to 7.7%, with year-to-date net absorption reaching 379,171 square feet (sf) reflecting continued leasing activity through the market. Aerospace, defense, mining, and small-bay users continued to drive demand, particularly in the Northwest and Airport submarkets. The largest lease was 36,212 sf at 3635 E. 34th Street, reflecting continued demand for functional industrial space in well-located submarkets. Development activity remained constrained as substantial vacancy still exists in recently completed new industrial construction coupled with rising construction costs, and elevated financing costs continued to limit new starts. Industrial construction costs increased again in 2026 after remaining relatively flat the prior year, driven primarily by tariffs on metals, followed by higher labor costs. High financing costs continue to hold back new construction, while tighter lending standards are limiting funding for marginally capitalized projects. Pricing Average asking rents remained stable at $0.92 per square feet (psf) per month NNN, with market conditions generally balanced as newer industrial projects competed for tenants. Limited available inventory of owner-user buildings under 20,000 square feet and investment properties continued to support strong pricing when placed on the market. Investment sale activity remained selective as lenders tightened funding for marginally capitalized projects. A notable transaction during the quarter was the sale of a 14-property small bay industrial portfolio, sold by Equus Capital Partners to Everview Partners L.P . for $165.75 million. Rising construction costs, tighter lending standards, and elevated financing costs continue to influence investment decisions and temper new industrial development. items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Washington, D.C. report here.HighlightsOperating conditions in the Washington, D.C., region were mixed in the third quarter as annual job losses narrowed for a second straight quarter and new deliveries slowed. Permitting reached its highest year-to-date level since 2022.Regional vacancy declined 10 basis points during the third quarter to 5.7%, the first quarterly decline in more than a year, though it remains 60 basis points above one year ago. Vacancy in the District and Suburban Maryland has eased for two straight quarters.Asking rents were unchanged from the second quarter at $2,233 per month but remain down 0.8% year over year. Northern Virginia rents were nearly flat from a year ago, and the decline in Class A rents has narrowed.Investment activity strengthened in the third quarter, with 16 properties trading for $1.8 billion, pushing year-to-date volume above the 2025 total. The year-to-date median sale price is $297,800 per unit.Washington, D.C. multifamily market overviewThe Washington, D.C., multifamily market showed further signs of stabilization in the third quarter as a slower pace of new deliveries coincided with easing employment losses. Vacancy declined for the first time in more than a year, although the improvement has yet to translate into rent growth. Northern Virginia continued to record the region's tightest vacancies and more stable rents, while the District and Suburban Maryland posted a second consecutive quarter of declining vacancy. Performance also varied across property classes, with Class A vacancy retreating and rent declines moderating, while Class C vacancy continued to rise. These trends point to a gradual improvement in operating conditions, though ongoing employment losses and uneven property performance continue to limit the recovery.Investment activity continued to strengthen across the Washington, D.C., region in the third quarter, with Fairfax County accounting for much of the increase in sales volume. Earlier in the year, transactions in Fairfax were concentrated in newer apartment communities, but activity shifted toward older Class B and Class C properties in the third quarter. These properties accounted for roughly three-quarters of the county's quarterly dollar volume. While sales volume in Fairfax remained near first-quarter levels, the county's median price declined from approximately $418,000 to $305,000 per unit.
