items.title: Las Vegas multifamily rent pressures persist despite leasing gains
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Las Vegas multifamily market report here.HighlightsLas Vegas multifamily operating conditions remain soft, with elevated vacancy, rising concessions and declining rents. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, but the improved supply-demand balance has yet to translate into rent growth.Stabilized vacancy reached 9.1% at the end of the third quarter, flat from the prior quarter but up 20 basis points from one year earlier. Vacancy remains 30 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month by the end of September, down 1.4% year over year and 0.9% lower than in the prior quarter, the second consecutive quarterly decline.Investment sales volume during the third quarter totaled roughly $209 million across five deals, with Class B properties accounting for four of the five deals. The year-to-date median sale price reached $225,900 per unit.Las Vegas multifamily market overviewLas Vegas multifamily fundamentals remain under pressure despite improved absorption and a slowdown in new deliveries in 2026. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries by roughly 650 units year to date, after trailing them by nearly 1,700 units in 2025. Absorption has already surpassed the full-year 2025 total, supported by continued job growth, while completions have slowed as fewer projects remain under construction. The recovery has been concentrated in the suburbs, where Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of that demand with less than half of the metro’s inventory. Rent growth has been slower to rebound. Asking rents remain below year-ago levels, with the steepest declines in older urban core submarkets, where vacancy is above 10%. By contrast, rents in suburban submarkets remain close to year-ago levels.Investment activity in 2026 has become concentrated in two of the suburban submarkets that are leading the leasing recovery. Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson accounted for roughly three-quarters of metro sales volume through the third quarter, up from 43% in 2025. Third-quarter activity followed the same pattern, with three of the five trades located in those two submarkets. Pricing has remained stable in Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson, with median sale prices near $250,000 per unit in both submarkets, above levels elsewhere in the metro, where recent trades have skewed toward smaller, older properties. The median price across the Las Vegas region has remained near its 2025 level, highlighting the influence of property location on pricing trends.Employment:Area employers added 21,400 jobs year over year. Image Area payrolls increased by 21,400 jobs year over year as of the third quarter of 2026, a gain of 1.8%. Hiring slowed from the first half of the year and held below the 10-year average annual growth rate of 2.4%.Professional and business services remained the leading source of new jobs, adding 10,900 positions and expanding 6.3% year over year. Education and health services added 5,400 jobs, while leisure and hospitality, the largest local employment sector, shed 2,200 positions, a 0.7% decline.Hyve Solutions, a manufacturer of storage and AI computing hardware, is establishing a new production facility in North Las Vegas. The project, the largest of four business expansions approved for state tax incentives in August, is expected to create 240 jobs over the next two years.Forecast: Employers are forecast to add roughly 20,000 jobs in 2026, a 1.7% increase, maintaining a pace similar to 2025. Development and permitting:Developers completed roughly 600 units in the third quarter. Image Developers completed roughly 600 units in the third quarter, all in Central Las Vegas. Year-to-date deliveries total around 2,600 units, down 23% from the same period in 2025. Roughly 6,100 units were under construction at the end of the third quarter, down more than 25% from the end of 2025, which is expected to ease supply pressure on operators heading into 2027. Six active projects in Spring Valley total more than 2,000 units.Multifamily permitting activity is regaining momentum. Developers pulled permits for 1,130 multifamily units in the third quarter, more than double the total from one year earlier.Forecast: Developers are expected to complete roughly 4,000 units in 2026, in line with both the 2025 total and the 10-year average.Vacancy:Vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1% Image Stabilized vacancy ended the third quarter at 9.1%, up 20 basis points year over year. Despite the annual increase, net absorption has exceeded deliveries in 2026, pushing vacancy down 30 basis points from year-end 2025.Class B properties account for roughly 70% of net absorption this year, with vacancy flat year over year at 9.0%. Class A vacancy edged up to 8.4%, while Class C, the only tier with negative net absorption in 2026, posted the highest vacancy at 10.0%.Suburban submarkets continue to pull away from the urban core. Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of net absorption this year, each with vacancy below 7.5%. Las Vegas Strip vacancy rose 170 basis points year over year to 12.1%.Forecast: Vacancy is expected to tick up 20 basis points to 9.3% by year-end 2026, though it would remain 10 basis points below the year-end 2025 rate.Rents:Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month. Image Asking rents averaged $1,479 per month in the third quarter, down 0.9% from the prior quarter and 1.4% year over year. Rents have declined for two consecutive quarters, erasing the gain recorded at the start of the year.Rent performance varied across submarkets. Henderson posted a modest 1.0% year-over-year rise to $1,580 per month, while rents declined in each submarket with vacancy rates above 10%, including a 5.0% annual drop on the Las Vegas Strip.Class A was the only tier to post annual rent growth, up 0.7% to $1,772 per month. items.title: Orange County multifamily rents continue to climb while vacancy holds
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Orange County Multifamily Market Report hereHighlightsConditions in the Orange County multifamily market remained stable in the third quarter, with vacancy flat while rents ticked higher.The vacancy rate held steady at 4.6% for the third consecutive quarter and is 20 basis points higher year over year.Combined asking rents for all classes, vintages, and locations of multifamily in Orange County increased 0.2% during the third quarter to $2,670 per month. Year over year, asking rents are up 0.6%. Year to date, multifamily investment sales activity is outpacing 2025, while the median sale price has increased nearly 20% to $365,200 per unit. The average cap rate across all property classes is 5.0%.Orange County multifamily market overviewProperty fundamentals in the Orange County multifamily market were little changed in the third quarter, with rents remaining near previous levels and vacancy holding steady. Deliveries remain elevated compared with last year, though the pace of completions slowed. This deceleration in supply growth occurred at the same time as a decline in absorption in recent months, keeping the vacancy rate flat for the third quarter in a row. Rent trends have been mixed in recent periods. While rents declined in several submarkets, the largest decreases occurred in Santa Ana and Anaheim, which had recently been among the strongest areas for rent growth. The recent decline appears to be more of a correction following outsized gains than evidence of a broader pullback in achievable rents.Multifamily investment activity has increased this year, with the market on pace to record its highest transaction count since 2022. Median pricing is also up from last year, although trends have varied by property class. Class A properties are trading at a median price of $425,500 per unit, down 7% from last year, while Class C pricing has increased 32% to $325,900 per unit. Class C assets have accounted for roughly two-thirds of all transactions this year, while only one Class B property has changed hands. More than half of all transactions have occurred in Anaheim, while Garden Grove has accounted for approximately one-quarter of total activity. Anaheim sales have been particularly concentrated, with every transaction occurring within a five-mile radius. Cap rates are generally ranging from the mid-4% to mid-5% range depending on property class and vintage.Employment:Employment increased by 6,300 jobs year over year. Image Orange County employment growth accelerated during the third quarter, more than offsetting some earlier losses. Employment increased by 6,300 jobs year over year, a 0.4% gain.The leisure and hospitality sector remained one of Orange County’s fastest-growing industries. Employment in this sector increased 2.1% year over year, with 5,100 new positions filled.The retail trade sector also posted stronger growth than has been typical in recent years. In the past 12 months, total employment in this sector increased 0.9%, with the addition of 1,300 jobs.Forecast: The current pace of employment growth is forecast to continue throughout the remaining months of the year. In 2026, total employment in Orange County is expected to rise 0.5% with the addition of roughly 8,400 jobs.Development and permitting:The construction pipeline spiked in recent months. Image The pace of deliveries in Orange County slowed during the third quarter, though year-to-date completions have already surpassed the 2025 total. Roughly 3,200 units have been delivered in 2026, more than double the amount recorded during the same period last year.The construction pipeline spiked in recent months, with projects totaling nearly 4,000 units breaking ground in the past three months. There are now nearly 7,400 units underway, up 16% from one year ago. Multifamily permitting slowed during the third quarter, though strong activity earlier in the year has kept year-to-date totals elevated. Through the first nine months of 2026, permits were issued for more than 2,500 units, roughly 50% above the same period last year. Forecast: Completion dates have been pushed back on a few properties, reducing the number of units that are expected to be delivered this year. In 2026, approximately 4,000 units are forecast to come online, up from nearly 2,200 units delivered in 2025. Vacancy:Vacancy went unchanged for the third consecutive quarter. Image The vacancy rate in Orange County was unchanged for the third consecutive quarter, remaining at 4.6%. Year over year, vacancy is 20 basis points higher.The city of Anaheim continued to be one of the best areas for vacancy performance in Orange County. Year over year, Anaheim’s vacancy rate declined by 60 basis points to 3.7%.Vacancies have also tightened in Anaheim, where the rate has declined by 40 basis points during the past 12 months, ending the third quarter at 7.6%.Forecast: Orange County multifamily vacancy is expected to rise modestly as absorption moderates, though market fundamentals should remain resilient. The vacancy rate is forecast to reach 4.8% by year-end, up 20 basis points from one year ago.Rents:Mission Viejo has the strongest rent growth. Image Following a second-quarter rise, rent growth continued in the third quarter, with the average asking rent increasing 0.2% to $2,670 per month. Year over year, asking rents are up 0.6%. Asking rents are now $3.09 per square foot per month.Mission Viejo took the lead as the submarket with the strongest rent growth. In the past 12 months, asking rents in this area increased 3.4% to $2,774 per month. Laguna Hills trailed close behind, with rents rising 3.3% in the same period to $3,005 per month.Santa Ana was one of the only areas to record a decrease in asking rents. items.title: Rexford Sells Fullerton Industrial Building For $50.2M: The Los Angeles Deal Sheet
items.description: Pexels/Tiger Lily Rexford Industrial Realty sold a 136K SF industrial property at 1500 S. Raymond Ave. in Fullerton to Terra Industrial for roughly $50.2M. Terra had previously been operating out of two facilities totaling more than 180K SF, “which presented operational inefficiencies and increased long-term occupancy costs,” according to a release from Cushman & Wakefield, which worked on the deal. A Cushman & Wakefield team of Kevin Turner and Jiselle Roberson represented the buyer. Cushman & Wakefield’s Randy Ellison, Brett Lockwood, Kyle McGillen and Andrew Ryan represented Rexford. PEOPLE Newmark hired Justin Rappel as a senior managing director, according to ConnectCRE . Rappel will be based in Newmark's El Segundo office, where he will focus on institutional industrial investment sales and joint venture equity placement. Rappel has more than 15 years of commercial real estate experience in brokerage, acquisitions, development and asset management. *** Kidder Mathews has hired Mac Hall to join the Solomon healthcare advisory team, based in the firm’s Century City office. The Solomon healthcare advisory team serves the western U.S. and Texas, specializing in healthcare real estate brokerage, with a focus on the veterinary, dental and medical sectors. Hall comes to Kidder Mathews from Accenture, where he was a client engagement manager specializing in marketing and advertising. SALES Marcus & Millichap announced the sale of the Knott-Orange Apartments, a 35-unit multifamily property in Anaheim. The 32,300 SF property sits on 1.25 acres at 515 S. Knott Ave. The property sold for $9.7M, or $275,714 per unit. The sale was the fourth from the same seller, which owns a multifamily portfolio in the greater Anaheim area and is seeking to rebalance its holdings through 1031 exchanges, the brokerage said in a press release. Marcus & Millichap’s Nick Kazemi, Tyler Leeson, Matt Kipp and Drew Holden had the exclusive listing to market the property on behalf of the seller, a family that had owned and operated it for more than 30 years. The team also procured the buyer, an undisclosed Southern California-based property management company. *** CBRE facilitated the $14.3M sale of a 56K SF office property at 20 Centerpointe Drive in La Palma. The sale price translates to $255 per SF. The single-story property sits on approximately 3.6 acres, was built in 1988 and includes approximately 194 parking spaces. At the time of sale, the building was approximately 84% leased to tenants including Convergint Technologies, ISEC Inc. and Telecare Corp. A local private investor acquired the property in a 1031 exchange. CBRE’s Anthony DeLorenzo, Sammy Cemo, Bryan Johnson and Jackson Marlow represented the unnamed institutional seller. FINANCING Gantry secured a $31M permanent refinance for the Valley Central Shoppes at 44410–44690 Valley Central Way in Lancaster. The 174K SF center is a component of a master-planned retail power center cluster and shadow-anchored by a Walmart Super Center and a Food 4 Less grocer. Gantry’s Tony Kaufmann, Jake Davis and Ramza Zeiter with the firm’s San Francisco production office represented the borrower, an unnamed private real estate investor. The 10-year, fixed-rate, nonrecourse loan was secured from one of Gantry’s insurance company correspondents. Gantry will service the loan for the lender. THIS AND THAT Architecture and planning firm MVE + Partners is relocating its Los Angeles operations to larger offices at The Bloc, in downtown's Financial District. The new location provides 60% more capacity than the firm’s previous space. MVE also announced 17 promotions, including five new principals: Luis Estrada, Paul Kearney, Raymond Albanesi, Tim Beuchat and Joe McClyde. *** Legacy Partners has begun leasing at Mill House, a 346-apartment complex at 2510 S. Euclid Ave. in Ontario. Legacy Partners built the project in partnership with DWS Group. Mill House holds 346 studio, one- and two-bedroom apartments ranging from 620 SF to 1,280 SF. Initial occupancy is anticipated in December, with construction anticipated to be fully complete in April. items.title: What's At Stake For CRE In Tuesday's U.S. Midterm
items.description: Last month, a 160-acre data center campus in Glendale, Arizona, moved a step closer to approval despite local pushback. Across much of Massachusetts, towns still won't let you build a single-family home on less than an acre. And in Florida, local mayors are bracing for a property tax cut that could blow holes in their budgets for police, fire and parks. On Tuesday, voters get a say in all of it. Bisnow/created with ChatGPT Control of Congress will dominate coverage of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections. For commercial real estate, though, most of the stakes are closer to home: the nine governor's races Bisnow is tracking in its markets, plus dozens of mayoral contests, utility board seats and ballot measures that will help decide where data centers get built, how much housing goes up and who pays for it. Data centers have become the campaign's favorite villain. Candidates and their allies spent $86.5M on TV ads attacking the industry from July through September alone. Politicians who once courted the sector now run against it. In Arizona, a former state lawmaker who backed data center tax breaks is campaigning against the facilities in a swing congressional district, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has gone from booster to regulator. The fights that matter most are playing out in statehouses and on obscure boards like Georgia's Public Service Commission, where two seats could decide how a nearly 20-gigawatt data center pipeline gets powered. Housing is the other fault line. With 80% of Americans worried about affordability, nearly every gubernatorial candidate in a competitive race is running on it. Voters will weigh fast-tracking environmental review in California, scrapping large-lot zoning in Massachusetts, and a property tax cut in Florida that could hurt Miami’s in-migration . In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani is asking voters to collapse 40 construction approvals into one. Below is every race and measure Bisnow is tracking with CRE stakes, market by market. ARIZONA Phoenix has emerged as a hot spot for data center development, home to 149 of Arizona’s 160 facilities , and just last month, a 160-acre planned campus in the West Valley moved closer to approval . As citizens increasingly raise concerns about their negative impacts, the gubernatorial race could determine what that landscape looks like going forward. Whether Democratic incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs or Republican challenger U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs wins, a moratorium is likely off the table , despite calls for it from lower levels of government. Hobbs signed a budget bill in June that imposed a three-year freeze on new sales tax breaks for the facilities. Two months later, Attorney General Kris Mayes, also running for reelection, called for a statewide pause on data centers. But Hobbs said a moratorium isn’t a way forward for the state. “I think there are places where data centers make sense, and they're an important part of the high-tech economy that we're growing here,” she said in September, according to ABC . Biggs has said local communities should have the final say on data center moratoriums. Former state Rep. Amish Shah supported tax breaks for data centers in the past , but now he is running on opposing the facilities in a bid to win over voters. Shah faces Republican candidate Jay Feely for Arizona's 1st Congressional District seat, one of a handful of races that could decide which party controls the House. CALIFORNIA Californians are voting on Proposition 45, which will decide whether to set timelines for environmental reviews and approvals on eligible “essential” projects, including roads, housing, schools, transportation and broadband internet. It would also set a deadline for courts to make decisions on applicant challenges to unfavorable decisions on these projects. If passed, it could have big implications for multifamily projects across California. The state will also be replacing the termed-out Gavin Newsom with either Democrat Xavier Becerra or Republican Steve Hilton. Both candidates agree affordability is a critical issue facing California but have different plans for tackling the problem, including how they would approach lowering the cost of housing and decreasing developer costs . In Los Angeles, incumbent Mayor Karen Bass is facing Nithya Raman, a sitting council member and former Bass ally. In her tenure, Bass issued executive directives aimed at streamlining the production of affordable and market-rate housing. Raman, the former chair of the Housing and Homelessness Committee, has proposed additional tweaks that she says would ​​triple annual housing production of all kinds in the city. FLORIDA Florida voters are picking the first new governor since 2019, deciding between Republican candidate Byron Donalds and Democratic candidate David Jolly to succeed Ron DeSantis. The state’s real estate community is overwhelmingly behind Donalds, who called for the removal of local zoning restraints to boost housing inventory, said the state should seek technology to modernize permitting systems, backs increasing the state’s homestead exemption, and has expressed support for changing Fannie Mae’s condo lending rules. Jolly has called for greater local control over zoning and development, wants more state investment in affordable housing, and seeks to remove hurricane and wind risk from the private insurance market to help lower premiums. Florida voters will also vote on Amendment 3, which would significantly cut homeowners' property taxes. If passed, up to $250K would be exempt from property taxes by 2028, compared to the current $50K. It has drawn criticism from localities that could lose millions of dollars, jeopardizing their ability to fund local hospitals, police, fire, parks and water management. South Florida developer and billionaire Jorge Pérez has warned a drastic cut to essential infrastructure funding could threaten Miami’s ability to attract and retain residents. items.title: The Data Center Election That Matters Isn't In Congress
items.description: Data centers have become one of the nation’s defining political issues ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. As tech giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to build behemoth facilities and use vast amounts of power to support their artificial intelligence race, communities have pushed back. Candidates on the federal, state and local levels have responded to data center opposition by proposing stringent regulations on the industry — and by painting their opponents as data center supporters. This contentious issue could influence the control of Congress and reshape statehouses across the country. Bisnow/created with ChatGPT But for all the focus on data centers on the campaign trail, industry experts say the election’s actual impact on the development boom may be less widespread than the rhetoric would suggest. In Congress, even if a wave of anti-data center Democrats take control of both chambers, they would still struggle to pass significant legislation that could receive the signature of President Donald Trump , a vocal supporter of the industry. In many states, candidates on both sides of the aisle are supporting stricter data center rules — meaning the industry is in for a tougher road no matter who wins. But there are state-level races in the key digital infrastructure markets of Texas, Pennsylvania and Georgia where candidates have staked out different positions, and the election could determine how much data center development will be allowed to move forward. Just in those three states, Morgan Stanley estimates the planned development of 284 data centers totaling more than 33 gigawatts of capacity are at risk pending the results of these races. “I don't think at the federal level the policy is going to shift much,” MOCA Economics Chief Economist Brandon Michalski told Bisnow . “If we go to the state level, that shifts dramatically and could change the trajectory significantly.” The Battle For Capitol Hill From Ohio and Michigan to Wisconsin, Texas and Maine, data centers have emerged as a major campaign issue in high-profile House and Senate races ahead of this week’s midterms. Data centers are deeply unpopular , and congressional candidates from both parties have made proposals to rein in development or limit its impacts a core element of their campaigns as voters voice growing concerns over electricity costs, environmental impacts and the broader consequences of the AI data center boom. The trend is especially visible in political advertising . As of the beginning of October, House and Senate campaigns had spent more than $29M on ads mentioning data centers, almost always negatively, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Bisnow . Although opposition to data centers cuts across party lines, Democrats have more aggressively nationalized the issue, contrasting calls for oversight of the sector with the Trump administration’s support for accelerating AI infrastructure development. Prominent congressional Democrats have already proposed measures like a national data center moratorium and released an investigation arguing that hyperscalers aren’t paying their fair share of grid costs. Now, party leaders are signaling their intent to make more aggressive oversight of the industry a prominent part of their policy agenda following the midterms, particularly if the party gains control of one or both houses of Congress. Last week, the Senate’s top Democratic tax writer announced plans to pursue an additional excise tax on data centers while eliminating the industry’s ability to tap a range of existing tax benefits tied to depreciation, research spending, opportunity zones and REIT structures. Although Republicans have also pursued measures aimed at addressing voter concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices, GOP leaders have privately acknowledged that data centers have become a winning issue for Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned major technology and AI firms in August that Democrats were successfully making data centers the “centerpiece” of the Senate race in Ohio and that deteriorating public sentiment toward the industry was becoming a broader risk to Republican candidates specifically. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” the letter warned . The data center industry has taken notice of this partisan dynamic. AI infrastructure super PAC Leading the Future and connected groups have spent significantly more supporting Republicans than Democrats, according to Forbes , while hyperscalers and AI giants like OpenAI have reportedly ramped up lobbying in anticipation of more aggressive Democratic oversight of data center development and the AI trade. Investors and analysts focused on the data center industry have similarly warned that the potential for Democratic victories in the House and Senate poses a threat to the industry’s growth and would bring greater regulatory and political risk. “There will be congressional hearings. There will be investigations,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel , according to Reuters. “You never know where that stuff leads, and there can be negative headlines.” Yet despite the rhetoric and the flood of money pouring into congressional races, not everyone is convinced that even a Democratic sweep would materially change the federal regulatory environment for data centers. A report published this week by MOCA Economics examining data center construction spending projected that Democratic control of at least one chamber would be a “nothingburger for policy.” Michalski, who authored the report, said Democrats could introduce more restrictive bills, but Trump’s veto power would make measures such as a national moratorium, sweeping new grid cost requirements or additional tax burdens extremely difficult to enact. items.title: HOUSTON HOMEBUYING ACTIVITY EASES IN SEPTEMBER AS MORTGAGE RATES RISE
items.description: HOUSTON HOMEBUYING ACTIVITY EASES IN SEPTEMBER AS MORTGAGE RATES RISE Home prices remain steady as buyers navigate elevated mortgage rates HOUSTON -- (October 14, 2026) -- As Houston's housing market moved into the fall season, homebuying activity eased compared to a year ago as buyers faced mortgage rates greater than 7%. Despite higher borrowing costs, home prices remained steady. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' September 2026 Housing Market Update, 7,030 single-family homes were sold, down 5.7% from a year earlier. The average home price edged up by 0.7% to $421,311. The median price, which represents the midpoint of all homes sold, was essentially unchanged at $325,000. Buyers had more choices than they did a year ago. There were 40,192 homes for sale across the Greater Houston area in September, up 6.3% from a year earlier. "Higher mortgage rates are making buyers look more closely at what they can comfortably afford," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "People are taking a little more time, weighing their options and focusing on long-term affordability. Stable prices and a broad selection of homes are helping keep opportunities within reach." Conventional 30-year residential mortgage rates averaged 6.86% in September according to Freddie Mac, up from 6.35% a year ago. Assuming a 20% down payment, buyers of median-priced homes in the Houston area saw monthly principal and interest payments rise from $1,622.29 a year ago to $1,705.41 in September. That's up $83.12 monthly or $997.40 annually. On a weekly basis, Freddie Mac reported average mortgage rates for September rising from 6.71% initially to 6.76%, then 6.95% and rising to 7.03% the final week of the month. Rates in the first two weeks of October continued to climb to 7.28% and then 7.40%, respectively. Housing Market Overview Across all property types, 8,181 properties were sold in September, down 6.4% from a year ago. Total dollar volume reached $3.45 billion, which is down 2.1% from the same time last year. Active listings across all property types rose 5.0% to 62,002 available properties. Single-Family Homes Update In September, single-family home sales totaled 7,030, down 5.7% compared to a year ago. The average sales price rose from $418,256 to $421,311. The median price edged down from $325,990 to $325,000. Inventory expanded from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. Nationwide, there was a 4.8 months supply, according to the National Association of Realtors. Homes took an average of 58 days to sell, compared with 56 days a year ago. Pending listings, which represent homes under contract but not yet closed, declined 11.6% to 6,789. This suggests some buyers are taking more time before committing to a purchase. Broken out by housing segments, single-family home sales performed as follows: $1 - $99,999: increased 3.7% (111 transactions) $100,000 - $149,999: increased 5.6% (188 transactions) $150,000 - $249,999: decreased 8.4% (1,359 transactions) $250,000 - $499,999: decreased 5.7% (3,878 transactions) $500,000 - $999,999: increased 0.6% (1,189 transactions) $1M and above: decreased 8.2% (304 transactions) HAR also reports on existing single-family home sales, which held steady compared to last September with 5,062 closings. The average price declined 1.1% to $427,110, while the median price was unchanged at $325,000. HAR will publish its September 2026 Rental Market Update on Wednesday, October 21. For HAR's Monthly Activity Snapshot (MAS) of the September 2026 trends, please CLICK HERE to access a downloadable PDF file. Townhome/Condominium Update The townhome and condominium market faced stronger headwinds in September. Sales declined 21.0% from a year ago, with 323 properties sold. The average sales price decreased 4.6% to $261,052. The median price fell 9.1% to $209,000. Active listings rose 6.9% to 3,609 available properties. Inventory rose from 8.0 months to 9.3 months. Pending sales declined 15.9%, from 440 to 370. Houston Real Estate Highlights in September • Single-family home sales decreased 5.7% year over year. • Pending sales declined 11.6% to 6,789. • Active listings increased 6.3% to 40,192 homes. • Days on Market for single-family homes increased from 56 to 58 days. • The single-family average price increased 0.7% to $421,311. • The single-family median price remained essentially unchanged at $325,000. • Inventory expanded from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. • Total property sales declined 6.4% with 8,181 transactions. • Total dollar volume decreased 2.1% to $3.45 billion. items.title: HOUSTON RENTERS FIND MORE OPPORTUNITIES IN AUGUST
items.description: HOUSTON RENTERS FIND MORE OPPORTUNITIES IN AUGUST HOUSTON -- (September 16, 2026) -- Renters in the Greater Houston area continued to benefit from a stable rental market in August. More homes were leased while rent prices remained virtually unchanged from a year earlier. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' August 2026 Rental Market Update , leased listings of single-family homes totaled 4,805, up 4.7% year over year. A healthy level of active listings helped keep pricing steady. The average lease price for a single-family home was $2,412, nearly flat compared to $2,414 in August 2025. Homes took 36 days to lease, one day longer than last year. "The rental market remained well-balanced in August," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "Having more choices at stable price points helps renters focus on finding a home that meets their needs. As we move into the fall, renters should continue to find a market that offers both opportunity and flexibility." Renters considering townhomes and condominiums had more options in August. New listings rose 1.9% year over year to 1,228 units, and active listings increased 9.0% to 2,304, giving renters more options in this segment of the market. Leased listings totaled 717 properties, down 2.7% from August 2025. Townhome and condominium lease prices moved higher, with the average lease price rising 2.4% to $2,014. Properties also leased slightly faster, with Days on Market improving from 48 to 45 days. items.title: The Rate Path Wildcard (October 2026 Housing Market Forecast)
items.description: The Rate Path Wildcard (October 2026 Housing Market Forecast) Written by Mischa Fisher on October 23, 2026 The decline in existing home sales is forecasted to accelerate in the fourth quarter, as our moving average of newly pending existing home sales dropped 12.8% in Zillow's latest weekly data. Total annual sales are still forecasted to finish up slightly in 2026 relative to 2025, given the lower share of sales volume the fourth quarter contributes. Inventory growth is expected to increase 6.6% Y/Y in Q4, alongside home value growth of only 0.7% Rent growth is continuing to build, with rents expected to grow 2.4% in multifamily and 3.2% in single-family in the fourth quarter. Given the volatility in mortgage rate paths, mathematical models are more likely to require revision. As we’ve continued to note in a variety of commentary : the current economic cycle is a strange one. We’ve added a rate hiking cycle with its expected contractionary effects on top of a weak housing market rather than on top of a strong market, defying the normal story we expected from Ed Leamer’s characterization that housing is the business cycle. As a result we’re expecting October existing home sales (we’ll release full month statistics on November 5th ) to be down considerably year-over-year. (On a rolling average weekly basis, newly pending listings dropped a whopping 12.8% year-over-year in our latest weekly data ). But the most important question right now for both housing and the economy is what else is slowed by high interest rates, and how soon. If the past is prologue we expect at some point a return to more normal market dynamics, where housing leads the business cycle. This necessarily means something else in the economy would need to slow first, the question is when. For example, we’ve seen recent selloffs in the AI related equity market paired with some nervousness about expectations for return on invested capital. So if this or another part of the economy outside of housing does indeed slow, then we’d expect investors to migrate to the safety of longer dated securities, mortgage rates to come down, home sales to rise, and housing to lead the business cycle again. But while there are early signs of this, it hasn’t happened yet. So while our current outlook is based on the current rate path, I think it’s increasingly likely that the actual path we follow will either be notably better or worse than what the math would predict. (Worse, if inflation isn’t brought under control, or better if inflation and/or growth expectations drop sooner rather than later). With that caveat on the current math noted, here’s what our latest forecast predicts. items.title: Renters: Results from the Consumer Housing Trends Report 2026
items.description: Renters: Results from the Consumer Housing Trends Report 2026 Edward Berchick Written by Edward Berchick on October 22, 2026 Key Highlights About 35% of households live in rented homes. About 23% of them moved in the past year. Roughly 78% of recent renters use AI, and most who do apply it directly to their housing search (recommendations, lease Q&A, market insights), with 60% saying they'd trust AI-personalized guidance. About 3 in 4 recent renters pay a recurring fee (76%), yet nearly all want fees disclosed upfront (96%) and folded into total rent (78%) rather than tacked on separately. About 30% of recent renters cried during their search. Renters are heavily digital throughout their homefinding journey (81% used a mobile website, 72% used an app, and the typical recent renter used 5 sites), but not completely: 85% still attend at least one in-person tour. For more on how we ran the survey, see the full methodology . The Typical Renter & Rental In this section, we provide a high-level overview of renters and what their homes look like. According to the Census Bureau 2024 American Community Survey , 35% of households live in rented homes. About a fifth of those rental households (23%) moved in the past year . The demographic estimates in this section for “renters” and “renter households” represent the rental household decision makers (head of household, their spouse/partner, and roommates). In cases where a household has multiple decision makers, the demographic characteristics are representative of an average or midpoint of all decision makers in the rental household. Age The median age of a renter is 41 years old and about half of renters are under the age of 40; only 8% of renters are in their seventies or older, and 16% are in their sixties. In other words, the age distribution of renters trends younger than the overall US population. Renters who did not move in the last year trend older than those who did move. The median age for a tenured renter is 43 years old -- a decade older than the typical renter who moved (33 years old). Recent renters are more likely to identify as LGBTQ+ (15%) than tenured renters (11%) or renters as a whole (12%).
